RODDICK (Montreal, St. Antoine) moved second reading of Bill (No. 11) to provide for the establishment of a medical council in Canada. He said : Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of the Bill for the establishment of a medical council in Canada it is my desire to be brief, because I had an opportunity last session in this House of explaining this measure very fully, and besides, I understand several hon. gentlemen wish to speak upon this subject. My main object for framing this Bill for the establishment of a medical council in Canada is for the purpose of establishing a qualification for medical men which would be acknowledged and accepted in all parts of the Dominion of Canada. As you are doubtless aware, Sir, we have at present no fewer than eight examining and licensing medical bodies in this country. Some of these are doubtless doing good work and keeping up, or at any rate, assisting in keeping up the standard of medical education, but their usefulness is limited to the territories over which they have special control. Barriers have been erected, as you are doubtless also aware, Sir, around these eight territories so that it is practically impossible for a medical man, for a graduate in medicine, to receive a qualification to practice in more than one of the provinces. The barriers are so marked, so strong and so high, that very few indeed have the opportunity of representing the profession of medicine in more than one province. The frontiers are so closely watched, Sir, that we constantly hear of medical men being fined, and in cases where this fine has not been paid, imprisonment has been threatened for crossing a boundary river, or an imaginary line between two provinces, in order to serve and probably to save the lives of citizens of this Canada of ours. Therefore, Sir,
I contend that there is reason for interference on the part of this parliament. I be-

lieve. Sir. that section 91 of the British North America Act can well be evoked by this parliament in meeting cases such as I have mentioned. Section 91, which refers to the peace, order and good government of Canada, I contend, might well be brought into operation by this parliament in cases such as those I have cited. Such a state of affairs exists in no other country probably in the world. Even between the countries of France and Germany, I am credibly informed, a neutral territory of 15 miles has been marked out over which medical men may travel in the discharge of their professional duties so as to be able to assist the sick and wounded of either nationality. Therefore, I think it is time something was done in Canada in order to remedy so serious an evil. It may be asked why these unfortuuate men who have been fined do not take steps to procure licenses in the neighbouring provinces to which they are obliged constantly to travel. The reason is that it may be absolutely impossible for a man to receive a license in more than one province. If he has begun the study of medicine in one province and :f he matriculates in that province, he never can receive a license to practice in any of the other provinces. For instance, if an Ontario graduate, having changed his mind as to his domicile, having passed his examinations, wishes to practice In the province of Quebec, he cannot do so simply for the reason that the medical board of the province of Quebec insist that he shall begin by passing the matriculation examination of that board. Some of the ablest men in our profession to-day have been shut out from practising in Quebec and in Ontario where they might be very useful in hospital and professorial work.
Another object which I had in framing this Bill and in bringing it before the House, was to obtain reciprocity with Great Britain. That, Sir, can be done so soon as we have a central examining board for the Dominion. In 1886 the British Medical Gouncil enacted that:
On and after the prescribed day where a person shows to the satisfaction of the registrar of the general council that he holds some recognized colonial medical diploma or diplomas (as hereinafter defined), granted to him in a British possession to which this Act applies, and that he is of good character, and that ho is by law entitled to practice medicine, surgery and midwifery in such British possession, he shall, on application to the said registrar, and on payment of such fee (not exceeding five pounds), as the general council may from time to time determine, be entitled, without examination in the United Kingdom, to be registered as a colonial practitioner in the medical register.
The deflu ition states :
The expression 'British possession' means any part of Her Majesty's dominions exclusive r.f the United Kingdom, hut inclusive of the Isle

of Man and the Channel Islands; and where parts of such dominions are under both a central and a local legislature, all parts under one central legislature are for the purposes of this definition deemed to be one British possession.
That means that so long as the provinces are separate parts of the confederation, we cannot register in Great Britain as provinces. The British Medical Council will not undertake to look after the education of the various provinces, but I do state positively that so soon as we have a central examining board in the Dominion of Canada, the British Medical Council will at once accept the licenses from that board and allow our men to register immediately in Great Britain, or in any part of the empire over which the British Medical Council has control. That is a very important matter. It means that we would have open to our young Canadian medical men, the army and navy of Great Britain, as well as colonial appointments, many of which are very lucrative, especially in the Bast and West Indias. It will also open to Canadian medical men appointments under the British Board of Trade, so that ships surgeons may be appointed directly from this side whereas now bur young men have to go to England to first receive a license In one of the colleges of Great Britain before they can take a steamer across the Atlantic. 1 have here some letters from the management of the Elder-Dempser line which bears on the subject, and which I will ask the permission of the House to read :
Liverpool, February 27th, 1901. Messrs. Elder, Dempster & Go.,
Montreal, Que.
Dear Sirs,-We are most anxious Eo have Canadian doctors on board our Canadian steamers, and we want you to arrange it so. If wo have an English doctor on any of the ships, we want you to put a Canadian doctor alongside him to come to this end so that he may take charge of the ship from here.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) ELDER, DEMPSTER & CO. Liverpool, February 22nd, 1901. Messrs. Elder, Dempster & Co.,
Montreal, Que.
Dear Sirsi,-Canadian doctors. From what we have seen of these gentlemen we have the highest respect for them, and we are most anxious they should become practitioners on board our West African and West Indian steamers. Would see no reason whatever why Canadian doctors should not be allowed to sail with their Canadian diplomas on equal terms with English doctors. What is the next step to take? You will see we have written to the High Commissioner here and he says the only thing to do is to get the doctors to come to England fer examination. What does this mean ?
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) ELDER, DEMPSTER & CO.
Mr. Colmer, secretary to the High Commissioner, writing to Mr. Jones, of the Elder-Dempster line says :

February 21st, 1901.
Alfred Jones, Esq.,
African House,
6 Water Street,
Liverpool.
Dear Mr. Jones,-I duly received your letter of the 13th inst., in reference to the question of Candian medical men being registered m this country.	.
The difficulty is, as your medical superiu-tendant points out, that while the Medical Act of 1886 leaves the door open to Canadians, Providing the medical authorities in the Dominion offer similar facilities, the provisions of the statute have not yet been applied to the Do-
The only course for a Canadian doctor, therefore is to come to England for an examination whfch, if passed, will entitle him to registration. I return the inclosures to your letter herewUh'	x am, dear Mr. Jones,
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) J. E. COLMER.
Secretary.
This correspondence indicates how unfairly our medical men are treated, but we have' the remedy in our own hands, and that remedy is simply the establishment of a Dominion medical council and a central examining board in order to meet the requirements of the British Medical Act of lgg6. we have had numerous opportunities of testing the disabilities under which Canadian medical men labour during tins present South African war, and we have constantly heard of how medical men attached to Canadian battalions were not allowed to attend Tommy Atkins. U was in fact thought, that they were good enough to attend Canadian soldiers, but not good enough to look after English soldiers. That is a positive fact. Several of those gentlemen who have returned from South Africa have cited instances to me, and I have correspondence bearing on it wliicli I could produce if time would permit, showing that a great injustice had been doue to our Canadian medical men, and done probably to force our hand. Knowing as 1 do several members of the British Medical Council, I am satisfied that nothing would give them greater pleasure than that we should arrange in Canada here a scheme which would meet them half 'way. Other objects of this Bill of a minor character might be referred to, but X shall not touch on them at this particular time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in arranging a scheme of this kind, there is no intention; nor is there any necessity for any interference with the autonomy of the provinces. I am aware that the fear of such interference is the great objection which has been offered to this measure of mine. It is not intended to do away with the provincial boards in any way. They will still continue to exist as they have existed hitherto. They must exist for certain purposes. They must exist for the purpose of taxation and discipline. With the provincial boards will be left the question of taxation and all matters relating to the discipline of the profession. They will not be disturbed. Their autonomy will not be interfered with in the least degree. I would be the last man in this House to seek in any way to override the provisions of the British North America Act. I have the greatest respect for that piece of constitutional machinery, and I believe that any interference with the autonomy of the provinces is unnecessary and uncalled for in any way. Where the provinces wish to continue an examining board, as now, they can do so. I have no doubt at all that the larger provinces, that is Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and Manitoba at any rate, will each continue to have an examining board for the purpose of examining and licensing men who wish to practice in .i particular province only. For instance, a man who goes up before the Ontario Medical Council, when this Act comes into force, p8 X hope it will, may be examined by them as he Is now. They will undertake to examine him and give him a license to piac-tice in the province of Ontario only, and he cannot go outside of the limits of that province on that certificate. It will be the same in the province of Quebec. I think that for a great many years to come the system in Quebec will continue as it is now, but I have it on good authority that the smaller provinces will probably discontinue the examining of candidates who come before them. I state without hesitation, and without any detriment to the smaller provinces, that in the light of the present progress in medicine-judging from the rapidity with which some of the subjects^ at any rate are progressing-it is impossible for a man who is not a teacher connected with a university to keep up sufficiently well to be able to examine in these subjects. Among the provinces there are four which have no university-British Columbia New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and the North-west Territories; as they have as yet no teaching body, their men are not able to keep up sufficiently well to examine. On that account, and for the reason I have given, there is no necessity. I repeat again, for disturbing the provincial board and its present methods ; so it will continue as before.
This Bill, then, is a purely permissive Bill. It Is necessary, in order that it may come into operation, to have the consent and co-operation of all the provinces. It is necessary for the medical board in each province to go before the local legislature and ask for a short clause to be tacked on to the present Act. Every province has its medical Act. and it will be simply necessary to add to that Act something like the following-though it need not be in exactly the same words :-
When there shall have been established under the authority of the parliament of Canada a

111G
medical register for Canada, under the control of a medical council for Canada, then, notwithstanding anything contained in any of the Acts hereby amended, any person duly registered in the said register as a medical and surgical practitioner, or as a student of medicine and surgery, shall, without any further or other evidence of qualification, be entitled to be registered in the medical register of this province as a duly qualified medical and surgical practitioner, or as a duly qualified student of medicine and surgery, as the case may be, upon production of a certificate under the hand of the registrar of the said medical council for Canada, certifying that such person m so duly registered upon satisfactory proof of the identity of such person, and upon payment of such fee as may be prescribed by the medical council of the province in that behalf.
A short amendment of that kind, tacked on to the medical Act of each province, is all that is required to bring into effect the measure I am advocating.
Now, as to the scheme itself. How is this Act to be put into operation ? It is necessary, first, to have a medical council, which may be called the Dominion Medical Council or the Medical Council of Canada, which I think would probably be a better term. The composition of this council has been a great puzzle to those of us who have had to do with the framing of this Bill. It has occasioned me personally a great deal of thought and consideration. We have tried two or three schemes, which have all given more or less satisfaction, but which have not quite met the requirements. When I addressed this House a year ago, I stated that the plan which seemed to satisfy all the provinces was that three members of the council should be taken from each province -one appointed by the Governor General in Council, one elected by each provincial medical council, and, the president of each provincial medical council. That, we found, gave dissatisfaction in the larger provinces. The province of Ontario, with its 2,300 odd doctors, said, ' It is unfair to us to give us the same number only as the little province of Prince Edward Island with something like 96 doctors.' Pressure was brought to bear so strongly that I looked for another scheme, and I think I have found one which will give general satisfaction. It is, that) for the first 100 or fraction of 100 practitioners in each province, there shall be one member. That will let in Prince Edward Island, and will also let in the xukon when it has a central board established. For the second 100 or fraction thereof over 50, there will be one member ; and for every COO above that, one member. That piinciple can be continued ad infinitum. Then there will be appointed members-one appointed by the Governor in Council from each province. There will also be university representatives, each university having a teaching medical faculty being entitled to send one, and there will be three homeopathic representatives from the entire Dominion.

I agree very largely with the promoter as to the value of this Bill to the medical profession. It is a Bill that is agreed to. I believe, by the six thou: sand medical men of the Dominion of Can-

ada almost unanimously. We liave been, ever since confederation, under disabilities in tbe various provinces, on account of the education of medical men by tbe provinces. In my opinion, it was an error to place the education of medical men under the provinces ; but with this I do not intend to deal. The education that is necessary for a medical man qualifies one that has received that education to practice his profession in any part of the world. We are not exactly in the same position as lawyers in this respect. Law differs in different countries, and even in different provinces ; and thus a person who may be qualified to practice law in one country or one province may not have the education to fit him for the practice of it in another. But, our profession being based upon the same principles, and our practice being the same, one who has received the necessary education is fitted to practice it anywhere. We are placed under disabilities in regard to our rights in the respective provinces of this Dominion. When we receive our diploma and license, these only permit us to practice in the province in which we obtain them. And if a young man-or an old man, for that matter-wishes to remove from one province to another, he is met with the Jaws of the other province, which exact from him, in most cases, an examination and the payment of a large fee. We believe that that is contrary to the spirit of the constitution of Canada ; we believe that when we spend four or five years of the best period of our lives, and pay also a little fortune, in order to acquire a profession, the license or diploma obtained should carry us a little further than the locality in which we live. Let me point out to you the difficulties which we experience at times. A large number of our young men go to our new western country to assist one another in developing that country. Among others is a certain proportion of young medical men who go. But as soon as they go they find themselves forbidden to practice until after they have complied with the regulations of the province in which they wish to settle. For instance, if a young man has received his diploma, let us say, from one of the Toronto medical schools, which require four years of actual study, and lias also passed his examination before the medical council of Ontario-a very high examination-yet, when he enters the province of British Columbia, where they have no teaching body, and where they are willing to accept a three years course, he must pass an examination and pay a fee of $100. Now, we think that a hardship. Let me give you instances. There were two young men of my own town who graduated in medicine a few years ago. One of them was a graduate of Trinity, who was the winner of a silver medal. He passed his examination before the medical council in due course. He decided to go out to the new country to practice his profession, and help, with others to,develop that new coun-Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
try. He arrived in British Columbia a few days after the examination had been held. He could not go up for examination for six months. It was impossible for him to remain in British Columbia spending money and doing nothing for that length of time, so he concluded that it would be better for him to return to Ontario, which he did, and he is practising in Ontario to-day. Another young man in my town was thoroughly equipped in the medical department of Toronto University, having taken a high place in the examinations there. He passed the medical council's examination. He, like the other man, went to British Columbia. Being met with the same difficulty, he also decided that he could not wait for the examination, and, in any case, he had not $100 to pay his fee. This result was that he went to California and established himself there. He is practising in California to-day, and Canada has lost a very good citizen. In order to overcome these disabilities, Canadian medical practitioners wish to establish the Dominion Medical Council before which any person who wishes to practice in any of the provinces outside of the one in which he has taken his diploma may come and obtain a diploma which will give him the right to practice in any province of the Dominion. As the promoter of the Bill has very truly pointed out, when medical practitioners are living near the border line between provinces, they may be called in cases of emergencies to treat persons on the other side of the provincial line. And, medical men have actually been fined for going across the border to treat persons in cases of emergency. Such a case happened within a few miles of this very city of Ottawa. A medical man of the city of Ottawa, no matter how high his qualifications, cannot cross the interprovincial bridge at the Chaudiere to treat a person on the other side of the river. Now, such anomalies, I think, should not prevail in a country where we have such large views of nationality.
Then, again, we are hampered, as the doctor has pointed out, by our position in the British possessions. Medical men from Australia, and from its various divisions previous to the establishment of the Commonwealth, were permitted to register under the General Medical Act of Great Britain, and therefore could qualify themselves to occupy any position they might receive in the civil service, the navy, the militia, or the service of the East Indian Company ; in fact, any position in the gift of the British government, could be bestowed upon those gentlemen living in Australia, British India, the British West Indies, South Africa, and New Zealand. But the graduates from Canada were denied that privilege because they were not graduates of a British possession as defined in the British Medical Act. My hon. friend from Montreal made reference to this matter, but allow me to read the clause under which the graduates of other colonies register in Britain, and the one un-

der which the graduates of Canada wish, under this Bill, to register. This is the article in the Medical Act passed in 1896 by the British parliament, which relates to that matter :
On and after the prescribed day where a person shows to the satisfaction of the registrar of the General Council that he holds some recognized colonial medical diploma or diplomas (as hereinafter defined) granted to him in a British possession

Now, note the expression ' British possession.'

to which this Act applies, and that he is
of good character, and that he is by law entitled to practice medicine, surgery and midwifery in such British possessions, he shall, on application to the said registrar, and on payment of such fee not exceeding five pounds as the General Council may from time to time determine, be entitled, without examination in the United Kingdom, to be registered as a colonial practitioner in the medical register.
Now, that is the privilege extended by this Act to medical graduates in a British possession. But if we turn to section 17 of this Act, we see the definition of a British possession and by that definition Canadian graduates are shut out from the right to register under the British Medical Act. This is the definition in the clause that shuts us out :
The expression ' British possession ' means any part of Her Majesty's Dominions exclusive of the United Kingdom, but inclusive of the Isle of Man and the channel islands ; and where parts of such dominions are under both a central and a local legislature-
Notice, that is the position we occupy. -; all parts under one central legislature are for the purpose of this definition deemed to be one British possession.
Now, Canada is a British possession in the meaning of that expression, but Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, any or all of them are not British possessions; and consequently, as we are graduates of one or other ol' the provinces, we cannot say that our diploma is from a British possession, and therefore we are excluded from being registered under the British General Medical Act, and are excluded consequently from all those courtesies and advantages which would otherwise come to us. Now, for these reasons the general profession in Canada is unanimous in asking the parliament of Canada to remove these disabilities so that our practitioners may have the same opportunities of obtaining these positions in Great Britain as have graduates from the other colonies of that great empire. If this Bill is passed and crystallized into law it will be accepted almost unanimously by every member of the profession. There is nothing in the Bill from the preamble down to the last clause which compromises the interests of any party inside or outside the profession; and therefore I think that parliament would act wisely and judiciously, 36
would act in the interest not only of the profession but of all those who call the profession to their assistance, by passing this law and enabling us to establish a Dominion Medical Council before which students and practitioners might come to receive a diploma from a British possession, and thus they would be eligible to advantages from which they are now excluded.
Then again, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Montreal, this medical council is to be so composed as to be of great value as a consulting body to the government of Canada. The Governor in Council is to appoint one of its members from each province ; the members of the council from each province of the Dominion are to appoint one more ; then the universities which are engaged in teaching are to have the right of appointing one, and the medical profession will appoint the balance. So you see it is to be fully representative of the various classes of practitioners throughout the Dominion. It is representative of the Dominion; and because each province in the Dominion is to be represented on this council, therefore it will be representative of the provinces. When the advice of such a consulting body is required in regard to general health, epidemics or diseases, the government can call to their assistance these eminent men, who will be members of the council, and in this way the public at large will receive great advantage from the constitution of that body, a body the like of which does not now exist, representative of such large areas or of so many classes in all the provinces.
In view of all these facts, I am sure the House will agree, as I believe it is proposed to do, to submit this matter to a special committee, who will go over the various clauses of the Bill and see that each one is put into such a shape as not to affect prejudicially any class of the community. When the committee reports, and the Bill comes back to the House, and is submitted to a Committee of the Whole, any changes can be made which may be deemed necessary to make the Bill perfect and in the interest of the profession as well as of the community as a whole. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary for me t'o say any more. I think the considerations I have placed before the House are sufficient to convince hon. members that some change of this kind is necessary, and in the interest of the great profession which has given so much time and so much skill, without fee or reward, to promote the health and prosperity of this country.

speechtext:
The Bill which is now engaging the attention of the House is one that meets with my hearty support, and one which I think will meet with the approbation of every hon. gentleman in this House, whether he is a member of the profession or not. The hon. gentleman who has introduced this Bill and who



lias judiciously, during the last two years, held it over from session to session in order to have it perfected, is deserving, in my opinion, of great credit for the expenditure of time, of labour and of trouble which he has made in educating the profession to take the very progressive step the Bill is intended to accomplish. The subject matter of the Bill is one of considerable delicacy, and requires a good deal of diplomacy in its proper handling in order to harmonize the varied interests. Our educational affairs being under the jurisdiction of the local legislatures, the members of the profession in the various provinces have been jealous of their rights and privileges. The colleges and universities, the degree-conferring institutions, have been anxious to safeguard their present privileges. The various provinces have local laws which practically debar members of the profession in other provinces from invading their field unless they comply with these local laws, which are in many instances onerous and difficult to comply with.
Now Ontario is justly proud of the high standard and excellence of its medical education. For a long time the profession of that province stood out against entering into any arrangement for a system of Dominion registration unless their particular standard and regulations, or similarly high ones, were adopted by the other provinces of the Dominion. On the other hand the other provinces of the Dominion had laws which they considered useful to themselves and which they considered equally applicable to their particular part of the Dominion and they also took the same ground. The colleges and other degree conferring institutions looked at first with suspicion upon this movement fearing that their vested rights might be tampered with. All these difficulties had to be met and overcome. It has required years of agitation and education un-t'l now all the varied interests are practically a unit in assisting to secure the passage of this Bill. Viewed from a selfish standpoint, we, the medical men in the west, arc not so anxious that this legislation should be crystallized into law as those from the east. In fact, in many respects, looking at it from a selfish standpoint, it will be a detriment to us, but I am glad to say that the medical men of the west are not animated by any sectional feeling, and that they will join in any movement for the good of the medical profession at large and for the good of the public at large. The profession in the west is not at the present time in a congested state, although in the Northwest Territories alone, according to the report presented by the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Roddick), there have been more than one hundred practitioners who have gone into the North-west Territories during the last twelve months. That is a new country which is opening up and developing and population is flowing in so rapidly every year that we have not more medical men Mr. ROCHE (Marquette).
than the demand requires. However, in the east the supply more than equals the demand and new graduates must seek new fields in which to practise their profession and if they desire to practise under the British flag in the Dominion of Canada they must seek new homes for themselves on the prairies of the west. It is therefore of more importance to the practitioners of the east that this Bill should become law than it is to the practitioners of the west.
What an anomaly it is, as has been pointed out by both speakers who have preceded me, that a gentleman holding one of the best university degrees in the province of Ontario, probably a graduate of Toronto Univbrtsity, possessing special knowledge and ability, practising his profession in Ottawa, is unable to cross the boundary line, to cross the Ottawa river without being subjected to fine or imprisonment by incurring the penalties imposed by the province of Quebec ? And, vice versa graduates of McGill University, which is now turning ouII some of the best medical men on the American continent, men of standing in the practise of their profession, cannot cross an imaginary boundary line without being subjected to the penalties imposed upon them by the laws of other provinces. If it were a fact that the standard of medical education were so very much inferior in one province than in another there might be some excuse for such a law as this, but, the day has gone by when such a contention can be set out. It is not like it was in some of the states a few years ago when medical men were turned out by whole sale as goods are turned out of a factoiy. On the contrary, to-day, the standard is very high in each of the provinces of the Dominion and there is no possible excuse why such a law should be in existence at the present time.
Another feature that has been adverted to by the hon. member for Montreal is, that at the present time graduates from the different provinces of the Dominion are not placed on the same footing in the motherland as are graduates from the other colonies of His Majesty's dominions. For instance, a medical man who graduates in the commonwealth of Australia is allowed by simply paying his fee to obtain his license and practise his profession in the old country, while a practitioner from the province of Quebec, or the province of Ontario, must spend a certain length of time in the old country before he can go up for examination and then he must pass his examination and pay his fee before he can secure registration entitling him to practise. It is not because the standard is so very much higher in Australia than it is in Canada. I think we have as good colleges, if not better, in Canada than they have in Australia, but it is simply because of the lack of uniformity in our degrees in Canada. We cannot expect the motherland to recognize our

degrees from tlie different provinces when we do not recognize them between the provinces in our own Dominion, but, by having a Dominion registration board and allowing any graduate of any province to appear before that board, pass his examination and secure medical registration for the Dominion it will not only allow him to practise in any portion of the Dominion but to practise in the motherland as well.
By the passage of this Bill no vested rights are assailed there is no proposal to take away from any of the colleges or universities any existing rights or privileges. The Act is not a compulsory one to compel any one to pass the examination before the Dominion board. Any person graduating and desiring to practise his profession in a particular province has simply to comply with the laws of that province, but should he desire to place himself in a better position so that he will be able to practise in any of the provinces of the Dominion he may do so by appearing before the Dominion board, passing his examination, and securing the privilege of practising in any portion of the Dominion. There are one or two features in this Bill different from those contained in the Bill introduced during the preceding session to meet objections raised principally in the province of Ontario. One of these is in regard to the basis of representation and another in regard to the reregistration on a provincial degree. It was considered at first by the promoter of the Bill that representation on the basis of population would make the Bill too cumbersome and too unwieldy and it was proposed to allow each province the same number of representatives. To this there was objection made by the older and larger provinces that it would not give a fair show to the larger number of medical men in the larger provinces compared with the smaller number in the smaller provinces and a change has been made in the proposed Bill by which the profession according to population, as laid down by the hon. member from Montreal, are allowed representation. This, I think, will be satisfactory to the smaller provinces as well as to the larger ones. The other objection that has been made is owing to the fact that in Ontario, where the Medical Council is the examining board, they do not allow a graduate from, say Toronto University, to practise unless he appears before the Ontario Medical Council and obtains a license from that body. It is a very strict examination and they' consider that a graduate coming from Manitoba, having a degree from Manitoba University, should not be allowed to register before this Dominion board and go into the province of Ontario to practise his profession. A clause has been inserted, subsection 3 of clause 10. to meet this objection which reads as follows :-
The possession of a Canadian university degree alone, or of a certificate of provincial re-36*
gistration founded on such possession, shall not entitle the possessor thereof to be registered under this Act.
These are the two principal objections that were made to last year's Bill, and they have been remedied in the Bill as it now appears before the House. It is scarcely necessary to enter into a discussion of the various details of this Bill. I trust it will be referred to the committee that will be moved later on and that it will be thoroughly threshed out, where delegates from the various provinces will meet with the members of that committee. I believe that if this Bill becomes law it will not only be in the interests of the profession but also in the interests of the public.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the Bill introduced by the hon. member from West Montreal (Mr. Roddick), now under consideration, being referred to a special committee of the House, provided the principle of the Bill be not adopted now. Interested as we are in the welfare of the medical profession, we are still more anxious to uphold the constitution.
I believe that the most serious objection that can be offered to this Bill, is that it is unconstitutional. It is provided by the constitution that in each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects assigned to that legislature. If we except agriculture and immigration, both of which subjects come within the jurisdiction of both the Dominion and the Provincial governments, I submit that, as regards all the other subjects, this parliament has no jurisdiction ; and that were we to pass into law the Bill introduced by the hon. gentleman, we should be encroaching upon provincial autonomy. And even should this Bill be made to apply to the Dominion at large ; even were we to enlarge the geographical area of its operation, it does not follow that it would thereby become constitutional.
Let me call the attention of my hon. friend to Lefroy's work, 'Legislative Power in Canada,' and to the following quotation from Judge Burton's judgment :
I think the principle must he clear that neither the Dominion parliament nor the local legislature can attract to itself a jurisdiction in matters assigned exclusively to the other power by the mere device of enlarging the geographical area so as to include the whole of the provinces, nor in the other case of restricting the area in which the power is to be exercised.
And Sir Oliver Mowat is quoted as follows :
It is clear that an alleged or supposed expediency of the law being uniform throughout the Dominion on any subject which is otherwise within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures does not give jurisdiction to the federal parliament to create uniformity.
Further on, the Hon. Edward Blake is quoted as saying :

We must recognize as an inconvenience inseparable from the federal system a lack of power anywhere to make uniform regulations, co-extensive with the whole Dominion, on subjects relegated to provincial authority.
Now, if we return to the British North America Act, we see that under clause 92, subsection 13, the legislature is empowered to exclusively make laws in relation to property and civil rights in the province ; surely, the right of practising medicine in another province is a civil right, and therefore, the parliament of Canada cannot pass into law such a Bill as is now under consideration.
Under clause 3970 of the Revised Consolidated Statutes of the province of Quebec- and I have no doubt that similar provisions are in force in all the other provinces-it is provided that no person shall be entitled to practise medicine in the province of Quebec, unless such person has first secured a diploma from the Medical and Surgical Board of the province of Quebec.
Should we adopt this Bill, does it not stand to reason that it would conflict with the existing provincial laws ? So, if all civil matters, with the exception of agriculture and immigration, are relegated to the provincial authority, we are forced to the conclusion that the Bill of my hon. friend, desirable as it may be in other respects-and I agree that it would be much more convenient for medical men to have the right to practise in any one of the provinces-cannot be adopted. Moreover, another thing which clearly shows that this Bill is not within the purview of the powers of this parliament is that it contemplates the establishment of a central examining board and a uniform standard of education and examination. Now, is it not true that all subjects relating to education are relegated to the provincial legislatures ? At all events, only in such exceptional cases as are mentioned in the constitution is the federal parliament free to interfere. On these several grounds I say that parliament should not undertake to pass this Bill, as this is not the proper place to deal with such matters. After all, it seems to me that the various medical bodies of the Dominion could easily come to an understanding and form into an association, with a view to promoting their interests throughout the different provinces, without going to the length of having this association recognized by the federal parliament. With this end in view, they could bring their combined influence to bear upon the provincial legislatures, so as to secure some reciprocity in the practise of their profession. Such a reciprocity, for instance, has been brought about by the bar of the province of Ontario and the bar of the province of Quebec. We have in our respective statute-books provincial Acts under which barristers from the one or the other province are allowed to practise their profession, upon payment of the usual fee. For instance, not long ago, the solicitor of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was Mr. DEMERS (St. John & Iberville).
admitted to the bar of the province of Quebec, without having had to pass any examination, and upon payment of the customary fee.
Such a reciprocity existing between the two provinces, I say that it ought to be no difficult matter for the medical bodies to exert their influence, so as to secure from the provincial legislatures a similar privilege.
The main argument urged by the hon. member from Montreal, in support of his Bill, was that medical men cannot get a license to practise throughout the British empire. I think that on this point my hon. friend is also mistaken, and that he is putting a wrong construction on the British General Medical Act. As a matter of fact, under this Act medical practitioners in the British possessions, as well as medical men from foreign countries, are entitled to practise medicine and surgery in the United Kingdom.
Well. Mr. Speaker, I think Moli&re's aphorism : ' A door must either be open or shut,' applies here. Now, one of two things : we either belong to a foreign country or we form part of the British possessions : there is no getting out of that dilemma. The British Act applies to all countries, and my hon. friend is wrong when he says that it does not apply to the province of Ontario. Moreover, if we turn to clause 27 of the British General Medical Act, incorporated in our statutes, 50-51 Vic., we see the definition of the words ' a British possession and foreign countries.' If Ontario were not a British possession, it would rank as a foreign country, and even then, under clause 27 of said Act. medical men from- Ontario would enjoy similar privileges. Clause 27 reads as follows :-
The expression ' British possession ' means any part of Her Majesty's Dominions exclusive of the United Kingdom, but inclusive of the Isle of Man and the channel islands ; and where parts of such dominions are under both a central and a local legislature, all parts under one central legislature are for the purpose of this definition deemed to be one British possession.
In my view, this means the very reverse of the construction put upon the clause by the hon. gentleman. Is it not true that the province of Ontario is a British possession ? under the control of a central legislature ? To my mind there is not even a shadow of a doubt about it, and the hon. member for Montreal West has put a wrong construction upon that clause. Besides, as I said, if Ontario were not a British possession, within the meaning of the Act, then it would be a foreign country, and in that case medical men from foreign countries are entitled to the same privileges as are enjoyed by medical practitioners in the British possessions.
On these several grounds, Sir, although I do not object to this Bill being referred to a special committee, I do object to the principle of the Bill being now affirmed by the House.

(Translation.) Would the hon. gentleman kindly Inform me whether he has received any communication from the authorities of Laval university in connection with this Bill ? I ask this question because I was not in my seat when the hon. gentleman rose to address the House. A few days ago I got several copies of this Bill-and I may say that 1 have not had time to thoroughly examine it-and I sent them to the dean of the faculty of Laval university. As I have received no answer yet, it occurred to me that perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Demers) was speaking on behalf of the faculty.
(Translation.) I do not belong to the faculty of Laval university.

(Translation.) I may say that I have inquired, in a general way, of the hon. member from Montreal (Mr. Roddick) whether the members of the faculty of Laval university, were in favour of this Bill or not. From what I was told, I gather that the faculty has not taken a positive stand on the matter. I am further informed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roddick) that Dr. Laehapelle, the chairman of the Provincial Board of Health, and one of the members of the faculty, is a supporter of this Bill, but I have reason to believe that the faculty of Laval university is opposed to this measure.

(Translation.) 1 asked the hon. gentleman that question because, having sent the Bill to the faculty without receiving any answer, I wished to inquire of him about the position taken by the Laval professors.

There seems to be considerable doubt as to whether or not this Bill is within the purview of the powers of this parliament. The authority which has been cited by my hon. friend from Iberville (Mr. Demers) would tend to show that this parliament has no jurisdiction. At all events, even if this parliament had jurisdiction over this matter, yet in view of the fact that we know there is a good deal of jealousy on the part of the provinces which are at present exercising the same jurisdiction, I doubt if it would be well for us to legislate contrary to their wishes. As to the merits of the Bill, I understand from the discussion which has taken place to-day, that there seems to be some difference of opinion even amongst professional medical men. It is an old saying that doctors differ even in the exercise of their profession, and therefore it is not to be wondered at that they differ as regards legislation. I understand from my hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) that the only thing he has in view to-day is to refer the Bill to a special committee with the object of looking into its merits, and the law as well. It is a recognized principle that
when the House gives a second reading it approves of the principle of the measure, and but for the fact that my hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) has stated that his only intention is to refer this Bill to a Committee of the House; for my part I would not feel justified in supporting the second reading. But with the qualification which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roddick) has made, and with the object of further having the matter investigated and reported on later, I think the House will do well to consent to the second reading, reserving to itself the privilege of judging on the principle of the Bill when it comes before us for its third reading, if it should come to that.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
I wish to say that so far as I am concerned, that I do not share the doubts of certain hon. gentlemen as to the power of this parliament to pass this Bill. It is a statute jwhicli creates a corporation not having provincial objects, and on that ground alone I think that this parliament has jurisdiction to enact it. It is not an absolute test it is true, but would any of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject, venture to say that any provincial legislature in Canada would have the power to pass a statute of this character. I venture to think not. I believe that this parliament is the only legislative body in Canada that has power to pass such a Bill. A great many illustrations might be given from the very work that was cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Demers) to indicate that the weight of authority at the present time is not in favour of the principle which 1 understood him to enunciate. However, that question is not being debated just at present because the right hon. gentleman has consented that the Bill shall be referred to a committee for the purpose of being discussed there, and I suppose the question of its constitutionality, if we desire to discuss it, can be dealt with later on. So far as the merits of the Bill are concerned, I have not examined it very carefully, but there is one feature in it that appeals to me very much, and that is the principle of giving to the medical men of Canada a national standing which they do not seem to have at present. I am somewhat surprised to learn that an Imperial statute of the character referred to by the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Macdonald) has been permitted to exist so long, and that on account of it, medical men in Canada; men qualified to practise medicine in Canada have not been able to take the standing to which they certainly are entitled, in other countries, and particularly among our troops in South Africa. It seems to me that we ought to feel ashamed that medical men going from Canada; having the right to practise in any one of the great provinces of Canada; should in South Africa be submitted to the humiliation of not being allowed to attend the wounded among the

Imperial troops, simply for the reason that they have no standing among medical men in England. If I understood the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Roddick) that is the position our medical men serving in South Africa were compelled to assume. I, for one, as a Canadian, feel ashamed of that state of things, and I am prepared to advocate any reasonable legislation which will obviate so disgraceful a condition of affairs. As the Bill is going to a special committee and is to be considered there much more carefully than it can be considered in this House, I will not now take the time of the House stating further the reasons on account of which I am in favour of this Bill. I have not sufficiently examined it to say that I am in favour of all its provisions, and so I am confining myself entirely to the principle involved.

I was not in the House when the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Roddick) and the hon. Deputy Speaker spoke, but if, as I understand they made the statement that Canadian medical men were not allowed to treat the wounded in South Africa, I think there is a mistake somewhere. I certainly saw Canadian doctors treating the wounded on many occasion's.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read a second time.

Mr. JAMES CLANCY (Bothwell) moved second reading of Bill (No. 27) to further amend the Dominion Election Act, 1900. He said : Mr. Speaker, I Introduced a similar Bill last session, and as I then explained, the object of the measure is to prevent as far as possible a new and very dangerous system of intimidating voters at the polls. The object of the Bill is to prevent persons who have an interest in promoting the election of a candidate from going about circulating the report that the present ballot and mode of voting is not secret. It is no answer to say that the present ballot is perfectly secret, and that the voting is secret, because the persons who circulate that report know that it is secret, and therefore their crime commences the moment they set their statement afloat. I know nothing of more far-reaching influence than for persons to be permitted, at the time of an election, to go about saying to voters that the mode of voting and the ballot is not secret, and that it can be discovered how any person has voted who votes against a candidate who may be an employer of labour or is supported by an employer of labour. I will not take up the time of the House discussing this measure further, because it seems to me so perfectly obvious that it is necessary in the public interest. If we are to have anything like pure or fair elections on either side, we must meet these difficulties as they occur. The ingenuity of people in discovering new means of evading the law is so great and so frequently exercised, that we are constantly called on in this House to pass restrictive measures to meet such cases. To show that this Bill goes no further than we have already gone in protecting candidates and maintaining purity of elections, I will read section 118 of the Elections Act:
Any person who before or during an election knowingly publishes a false statement of the withdrawal of a candidate at such election, for the purpose of promoting or procuring the election of another candidate, is guilty of an unlawful act, and shall also forfeit the sum of one hundred dollars to any person who sues therefor, with costs.

I want to call the attention of the House to the fact that the person who circulates a report which he knows to be false uses a weapon for the purpose of intimidating voters. Now, all voters do not know that the ballot is a perfectly secret one, and it would be utterly impossible to convince some of them that there would be no danger of their losing their position if they voted in a certain way. I hope the House will see its way to accept this Bill as a proper measure for the protection of both sides, to guard against an evil which experience has shown to be one of the worst and most insidious forms of intimidation. I beg therefore to move the second reading of the Bill.

I would ask my hon. friend not to press this matter further at the present time. There are on the Order paper, some other amendments suggested to the Elections Act, and there are some others not yet introduced which we have to consider later, and I would ask the hon. gentleman to suspend his motion for the second reading of this Bill until we have time to consider all the amendments together. My hon. friend will bear in mind that this measure was proposed last year, and I think also the year before, and the House rejected it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: I am afraid the hon. minister rejected it.

I would not like to assume that my objection was the only one. At any rate, I want to consider the matter further in connection with these other matters, and I would therefore ask my hon. friend to let his Bill stand for the present.
I have no objection to let it stand, witli the understanding of course, that it will be considered with the other Bills.,
Certainly. Debate adjourned.

speechtext: What increase in the number of officers of the permanent corps has been made during the past year ?

During the time the contingents were serving in South Africa, a considerable number of permanent corps officers were in that country and had to be temporarily replaced. speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Would the minister be good enough t6 explain why a number of the officers of the permanent corps who are the juniors of many men in the militia-men of greater experience-have been promoted to the rank of colonel over their seniors ?

The officers of the permanent corps who have been gazetted colonel are Otter, Lessard, Drury and Evans. speechtext:
I agree with the hon. minister that these were proper cases for promotion to the rank of colonel, on account of their services, whether they were senior or junior. Could the hon. gentleman give me a list of all the promotions, including these gentlemen ?
The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEF'ENCE. I will bring it down. I understand that it is to include honorary colonels as well.

speechtext: He was not a departmental officer, but it was his duty to pay out the money. If the hon. minister has any means of getting the information, I shall be glad to have it. I will apply for it privately.

As I understood the hon. minister those officers who had been mentioned in the despatches of the British general were given the rank of colonel. But why were not all officers who were equally creditably mentioned in these despatches given the rank of colonel ?
