speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I must enter my emphatic protest against the attempt that is being made-I shall not blame the minister for it-but the department, the red-tapeism of the department to give undue prominence to the permanent corps. It was so when those who are now in opposition in this House were in power, and I presume it will be so until the end of the chapter. Ever since the establishment of the permanent corps, there has been an attempt on the part of the gentlemen in that corps to place it superior to the active Hon. Mr. BORDEN (King's).
militia. There is a fear-a well-grounded, properly-grounded fear-not; only on the part of the active militia, but on the part of the men on the side lines who pay the taxes of this country, against what' they are pleased to term the spirit of militarism. They dread anything in the shape of an active militia regiment being established in their locality for fear of strengthening that spirit. Now, we have fought for years-I fought when my own friends were in office- against giving prominency to this permanent corps. We were told :	These gentlemen will understand the drill-book and drill better than an ordinary militiaman. Why, there is not a school boy, there is not a page on this floor, but could read in a week all the books that these gentlemen have to read. And, for a man of ordinary intelligence holding a position in the active militia of Canada to become perfect in -the book knowledge that is required to command a pennant corp or a militia corp in this country is a very easy, and a very simple matter. There are scores of men throughout the length and breadth of this country who are infinitely better posted than the men of the permanent corps. I can tell you, Sir, that some of the gentlemen whom this government has been pleased to create full colonels, when proceeding to active service in South Africa did not know the difference between a hired ship and a regular military transport. Further, officers in command en route to Africa-permanent corps officers, of course, for no man who was not a permanent corps man had any chance; officers of the militia, captains, and even men of higher rank could enlist as privates and have the privates of the permanent corps placed over them as noncommission officers, but when it came to commanding, all the positions of command were given to officers of the permanent corps-actually undertook to try the stewards of the ship, men in the pay of the captain of the ship. Why, they actually thought that they were the superiors of the captain of the ship. They did not seem to know that the captain could place the officer in command in irons if he chose- and the mystery to me is that, in some cases, that was not done. Yet we are told that these men are much superior to the men of the active militia of this country.
I want to point out to-day, as I have pointed out on many occasions in this House and out of it, that, from the earliest times in Canada until the present day, the irregulars, what you may term the active militia man, given as good arms and ammunition-in short, given equal opportunities with the regular-has trimmed the regular to a finish on every occasion. Take the history of the world, and it repeats the same thing over and over again. The defeat of regulars by irregulars in South Africa is only repeating the same story. The boys of the French Revolution period defeated the picked troops of Europe in every engage-

ment. In India, at the close of the eighteenth century, Britain had to find her Clive in a civilians office, and he it was who led her troops to victory. Again, at the time of the mutiny, she found her Nicholson, in the civil employment oT the empire, and he also organized victory for British arms. It was so in the United States during the civil war. Though the big positions were given to the regulars, the permanent corp men, the greatest success were due to the men from the farms. And even to-day the American nation finds in a farmer, a man who, three years ago was tilling the soil of Kansas, the man who in the Philippine war has brought it out of the wilderness, while the regulars, the permanent corps men of the United States have not proven equal to the occasion. So history everywhere proves that the irregular, the militiaman, given half a chance with the other, his individuality comes to the front and he proves himself a better man on every occasion.
I am free to say that the permanent corps men who will be able to tell off a drunkard may be a little better than an ordinary active militia man. He may be able to manage what is termed office affairs. He may be able to require the men to salute and go through the little etiquette, so to speak, of the service to better advantage than the men of the ordinary active militia. But that he is a better fighting unit for the defence of his country than the other, I am here to deny. I need not point to officers in this House who are fit to take their place in the command of men side by side with the best colonels in the militia of Canada to-day. I need not point to scores of officers in this country who are fit to lead their men in active service, or who are fit to lead their men in ordinary brigade parade, side by side with the officers of the permanent corps, and do it infinitely better than they. Let me relate what took place on a field day in the city of Toronto a few years ago. An officer, I think it was an officer of the Grenadiers, or of a Hamilton battalion, detached two companies in order to guard the other flanks. The attacking force came on, and the umpires, who were largely permanent corps officers, happened to see these companies detached at the flanks and they ruled them off the field. The only sensible move of the whole day was to put these companies there, yet they were ruled out of action by the permanent corps men, one of them an officer with the rank of Lt. Colonel in His Majesty's Imperial service. On being remonstrated with, it was pointed out that these companies would have been cut off instantly had they been in an actual engagement. Let me point out, Sir, that the magnificent Guards brigade at the battle of Magersfontein was held in check for more than half a day by seventy-two men of the Scandinavian brigade, although they did not occupy a position at all to be
compared with the position held by these two infantry companies of Toronto and Hamilton ; the magnificent Guards brigade were held in check for upwards of half a day by 72 men, about half the number that were detached from this Hamilton and Toronto regiment in that sham fight ; and, Sir, they held a position nothing like as strong as the position held by these people here. Again, I may point to an incident at Queenston Heights, where a permanent corps officer was in command, and where an ordinary hayseed brigade full of ordinary hayseed commanding officers
Order, order.
My hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) was not present.
But the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) was present.

Yes, I was. I make no claim to be any better than an ordinary officer commanding a hayseed regiment. But this permanent corps officer, after having made dispositions for defence, found himself suddenly surrounded with two battalions and a half of men on the Heights, within a hundred yards, although neither he nor one of his men had seen them go there. Again I can point to an incident in the past season where two permanent corps officers were acting as umpires to watch some companies occupying an impregnable position, much stronger than that held by the Scandinavian detachment at Magersfontein, and the companies were ruled out of order, although there were one hundred and there were only a hundred men opposed to them, by these permanent corps officers.
I would not bring these matters up were it not for a deliberate attempt that is continued year after year to put permanent corps officers in senior positions. I am not blaming the minister, it was begun long before he ever became Minister of Militia and Defence, and these evils then, I believe, were much more patent than they are to-day. But a constant attempt is made on the part of those interested in upbuilding the permanent corps in this country to place them superior to the ordinary militia force of Canada. I say that permanent force was created, not as a standing army, not as a police force, but it was created as an educational institution. Now, Sir, I stand here to-day to say that that permanent corps to-day does not perform the functions expected of it ; and if it does perform the functions of an educational institution, then, as a matter of mere arithmetic, if you take the cost of that force and divide it by the number of certificates issued, you will find every certificate issued to a young fellow from the country costs this country away up in the thousands of dollars-a rather expensive education. Now I wish to point out here in connection with the permanent

corps that they should be there as an educational force. I shall not discuss that matter any further at the present time, because I have a motion on the paper relating to it, and intend to discuss it at length when that motion comes up.
But I wish to point out to the minister that the militia of this country and the people of this country will not consent to see these gentlemen placed as seniors over men who have borne the brunt of the work of upbuilding the militia force of Canada and bringing it to the position it occupies to-day. There are scores of men in the militia force of this country who were in it almost before some of the men were born who are full colonels to-day. I am not saying anything against these gentlemen, but they are placed senior to the militia men, and I want to know what they have done for it. I may as well take up the question of military schools in connection with these permanent corps, although it will come up under another item. I may say that I took the same lines when the Liberal-Conservative party were in power on this question that X am taking to-day. I had the privilege of pointing out to a Conservative Minister of Militia and Defence in those days what I am pointing out to the Liberal minister to-day. I contended that the schools of those permanent corps as an educational institution, do not perform the functions that the people expect of them.
How does a young fellow get into the schools to-day ? I will give you an instance of a young fellow from a clean honest farmer's home, who becomes an officer in one of our militia companies. He wishes to attend the schools. He makes his application, but not being able to attend at the time fixed, he names another day when he wishes to attend. For instance, one young officer applied to go on the 1st of January. He was notified that he must attend on the 1st of November, or some date in that neighbourhood. It was absolutely impossible for him to go then, and as a consequence his transport was sent back. Two days before the 1st of January, when he had heard nothing whatever about the possibility of such an arrangement, two days before that date he received notice that he could attend school on the 1st of January. But the young fellow had made other ar-arrangements. He had been refused admission previously for the 1st of January, and had made other disposition of his time, and it was absolutely impossible for him to go then. Now supposing he had gone to the school, what would have been the routine procedure ? He would have had to purchase a little uniform. I am pleased to say that under the present minister and his predecessors there has been a little im-improvement-because after a few years of hammering away I did get our Conservative minister to relax a little on the red tape of the proceeding, but it took session after session of effort in* this House and in the Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
country to get the rule removed so that these boys from the country would not require to procure not only a full dress but a mess uniform before going to Toronto. We have got it down finally to something that is not very burdensome, but nevertheless they have got to buy a sword and a uniform, and they go down to Toronto, young fellows who know little or nothing about military work, and they are rushed into the ante room. There are certain little points of etiquette there that they have to follow. But these boys are not, many of them, in the habit of treating, or ' setting it up,' as it is termed. They are led innocently into violating this or that rule in connection with the routine of the ante room, and very frequently they are led into violating these rules by officers of the school, by officers of the permanent corps of this country, and then the punishment is ' setting it up ' for the boys. I can give you instances of young fellows whose fathers are rather averse, as a rule, to their boys entering into the corps, because there is a dread on the part of parents to see their sons rushed into this sort of thing. A young fellow has to haul out three, or four, or five dollars, as the case may he, and pay for ' setting it up,' in other words, for his little mistake in the ante room.
Tuttle things like that should be obliterated from every military school. I do not see that any advantage would be gained by a man going to the military schools of this country and living in the barracks. What is he going to learn by living in the barracks ? Our young men can go to the universities and medical colleges of the country and board wherever they choose throughout the city. Why should not a man in the military service be permitted to do the same thing ? The best men in the military service to-day were allowed to do this when they attended the old military schools. They were not obliged to go into the barracks and room with some fellow, possibly a decent fellow and possibly not. They were treated as self-reliant and responsible beings. To-day there is the old discipline of repression, the old spirit of dark ageism, and I shall discuss that point at more length on another occasion. The old spirit of repression is still in force. If we examine into the military systems of the nations of the world we find in them the remnants of dark age repression, of slavery, and of the discipline of the prison instead of the discipline of free men. Take our soldiers in the permanent corps to-day ; they are treated as children and not as men. I am glad to say the conditions are improving but improving slowly. I am sorry to say that the improvement is not making as fast progress as is the improvement in prison discipline. In the armies of France and Germany and the armies of other nations the discipline is being strengthened and an attempt is being made in this country at the present moment to fasten upon it the tyranny of a British

military system. I stand here to say that that will never succeed with a people living in a free country like Canada. Instead of the discipline being made more repressive, or continuing along repressive lines, it should be relaxed and men should be made freer. The discipline should be such as to promote freedom and individuality with the object of developing individuality rather than repressing it by enforcing the discipline of the slave and of the prison. I shall not take up the time of the House now, but on another occasion I purpose discussing this whole question of the training of ofiicers and I shall then enter into the subject at greater length. Mark you, however, the present hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Mr. Borden) deserves credit for having wiped out some of these objectionable features from time to time as they have been brought before him, or as soon as he possibly could. I am free to say that he has done a good deal in that line, but I would point out to him that there are a great many more reforms to be made in the permanent corps if we want the militia of Canada to be what it should be. I maintain that the militia of this country must always be the backbone especially in modern times with long range rifles. I shall not take up the time of the House by pointing out that long before the present war occurred I stated in this House that standing armies had to vanish. They must vanish under modern long range rifle practise and the only safeguard of any nation is to have the whole body of the people trained to the use of arms and possessing sufficient discipline to manage themselves so that they could easily get their positions. In that way the whole fighting population of the country could attend to business in time of peace and in time of war shoulder their rifles and march to the front, and by their expert marksmanship and overwhelming power, they would make a short, sharp war something that would only be possible in a country that has a great militia force. I shall not say anything more on this item until I hear from some other hon. gentleman.

The observations of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) are certainly entitled to consideration always. What he says on military subjects is entitled to consideration, and, I think, in view of his remarks in condemnation of the permanent force, he is entitled to receive from me some answer, if an answer is possible. I am glad to be able to agree with the hon. gentleman in all the good things he says of the active militia of Canada. I believe we have, in Canada, elements from which can be made as efficient a fighting force as can be found in any country in the world. The arguments, or statements, which my hon. friend has used against the permanent force, if they mean anything, seem to me to mean
that the permanent force should be immediately abolished. That is the only logical conclusion
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Why not reform them ?

The only logical conclusion to be drawn from my hon. friend's statements is that, as at present constituted and with the personnel which we find to-day in the permanent force, it is utterly useless, and of course, if useless, is really worse than useless if any strain were put upon the forces of this country in the way of demanding a defence. Now, I beg to differ entirely from my hon. friend. I cannot say that I am particularly in love with a standing army. I have said more than once that it is opposed, and I agree with my hon. friend that it is opposed, to the ideas and the wishes of the people of this country to have a standing army as such. But, we must have the nucleus of an army for the purpose of defence. We must have in certain permanent places garrisons, especially now when we are left entirely to depend upon ourselves. We must have teachers to instruct
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
To instruct the officers and noncommissioned officers of the militia force of this country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That is just what we want.

Very well. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that we have, taking it all in all, a good average set of men as officers of our permanent force, that they have done then-work fairly well and that they are doing their work fairly well to-day. I found, when I came into office, a certain condition of things existing in the militia, the result of development during some thirty years. I did not, after looking over the field, consider it to be my duty to wipe away all I found, although there were some things which I found which I did not approve of. I believed then, and I am more strongly convinced to-day than I was then, that the condition of things in the militia of Canada at the time I took office was fairly good, as good as could be expected in view of the money which had been voted from time to time and the attention which had been given to the militia. I have endeavoured, not to tear down or destroy, but improve, to build up and to add to the condition of things which I then found. Now, I most positively deny that the officers of the permanent force are men who are not entitled to the confidence of the people of this country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister say that I said the officers were not entitled to the confidence of the people?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What I said was that they were not more entitled than scores, I would say hundreds, of the active militia men.
Quite so, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) must remember that I have been trying to point out that we must have a permanent force in this country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The minister will be good enough not to place words in my mouth that I have never uttered.

I fail to see the point of the hon. gentleman's argument. He stated that on the occasion of certain military evolutions at certain points, the permanent force officers were not capable of commanding a brigade even.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I say so.
That is exactly what I thought the hon. gentleman said.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I say so.

Then, if we have in the permanent force ol Canada officers so ignorant that they are not able to fulfil the ordinary duties of an officer-to come back to the point I started with-the argument of the hon. gentleman means that we should sweep the whole force away as it exists to-day. Tlie hon. gentleman has made comparisons between the active militia and the permanent force, and he said the Militia Department had shown undue favours to the permanent force. To use his own words, he said : No man had any chance unless he belonged to the permanent force. Sly hon. friend knows, that of the officers that were sent to South Africa fully nineteen-twentieths of them belonged to the active militia. But perhaps my hon. friend will say that positions of command were given to permanent force officers. That is true. Positions of command were given to permanent force officers because it was thought necessary to place over the other officers and over the men sent to South Africa, men who had had experience, scientific and educated soldiers, men who had had the opportunity of being taught in the schools in England ; men who had had the opportunity-in time of peace, it may be-but whether in time of peace or not, had had an opportunity of continuous command in this country, and therefore should be more familiar with the duties required of them. These were the men who were selected. I Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
selected them on the recommendation of the general officer commanding. I have had no reason in any one case to regret the selection made. These officers went to South Africa and they did their duty with distinction to themselves and with credit to their country. Then as to the active militia does my hon. friend forget the record of the active militia officers who served in South Africa ? Does he forget Colonel Turner, who won the Victoria Cross and the D.S.O. ; does he forget Captain Cock-burn of Toronto
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: And Morrison of Ottawa.
Does he forget Colonel Hurd-man of this city, who was in a position of command ? Does he forget all those men who distinguished themselves ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Certainly not.

The argument of the hon. gentleman against the permanent force is not well founded. I think the House will agree with me, that we must continue our permanent force. While it is not perfect it is a fairly good force, and it is in the interest of the militia of this country that we should maintain it. As to the schools, the hon. gentleman has said that the principal object of the permanent force is education.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

There is no question about that. But the hon. gentleman has said that there are some difficulties found at the schools, and he objects to our insisting upon the officers from the active militia to be required to live in barracks.	.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The minister has misunderstood me. My chief objection to the officers living in barracks is this : That you can only pass a very few officers at very great expense. I am not specially objecting to men living in barracks, although I have yet to see the advantage of a man living in barracks over a man living outside.

There would be I suppose the same advantage as in the case of a student attending a university, who has the advantage of living within the walls of the college. He has an advantage over the student who lives outside. When a man lives in barracks there is a military atmosphere pervading
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Pretty thick sometimes.

However that may be, there is the advantage of lectures, there is the advantage of constant association with military officers, there is the advantage of the

officers being attached for duty, as they are in many cases, so that they may learn their duties by actual experience. I agree with the hon. gentleman in the main, that it is desirable to give much wider opportunities to the officers of the active militia to acquire knowledge, and that we should when possible carry the schools to the officers at certain centres. That we have done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Yes, I know.

That was done by the former government and we have continued it so far as possible, but the staff of the permanent force is limited, and it is difficult to carry on the schools at the depots and at the same time detail the necessary officers to carry on the schools elsewhere. But it is being done at all events to the utmost extent possible. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) spoke with regard to treating. Whatever might have been the case as to treating in the past, I believe that to-day, at the depots, treating is discountenanced altogether and it is against the rules.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I am glad to hear it.

An officer of the active militia who is attending the school is forbidden to treat, so that there ought be no objection on that score at the present time. When the hon. gentleman brings the question up on his motion, I shall be very glad to discuss the matter with him as fully as may be necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman seems to be under a misapprehension as to what I have said. The minister told us that one of the advantages of a man living in residence was that he would be attached for duty. Can the minister or any one else point out one duty that a re-sidental officer performs which under the old system was not performed by an officer boarding outside. I have had a military school experience and experience elsewhere, and I must say that the system of boarding outside the barracks was infinitely better both in a disciplinary sense and in the sense of being attached for duty. We had to get up in the morning and walk a mile or so and be in our places at 6 o'clock, and that in itself was good discipline. Then, every man had to be attached as a noncommission officer on guard duty, or canteen duty, or ration duty, or some other duty. There is no duty which an officer or noncommissioned officer performs in residence that he would not perform if he boarded outside. The minister certainly labours under a misapprehension when he: supposes that I would sweep the whole force away. I would sweep it away as a standing army, but I would increase it as a
teaching body. I would entirely do away with the red tape and the standing guard. Why should you require to have a man standing sentry at the gate of your barracks. night and day, as if he were guarding the gate of a prison ? This is a free country. Our camping experience shows that those camps which have no guards are the orderly camps, while those which have guards at every tent door, hedging the men in, are the camps where there is disorder and where discipline fails. I do not believe in repressive discipline; I believe in educational. I purpose taking up this subject on another motion, when I will show that the training of officers is not being carried on at the present time in this country. We are not even keeping pace with the number of officers who are leaving the regiments. I venture the statement that there are fewer qualified officers in the force to-day, excepting those who have been qualified by their service in South Africa, than there were twelve months ago, and that there were fewer twelve months ago than there were twelve months before that. They are gradually falling off, and it is next to impossible to get an officer into the schools. But I intend to take this whole question up on another motion, and to enter into it at length.
Is the minister's report down yet ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I do not wish to stop the passage of these items; but I would not like to have the large items passed without seeing what the general and the officers say on the whole subject.
I expected to lay the report on the Table to-day. Would it do, as we have often done, to reserve one item for the general discussion ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That means that it may pass some night at 12 o'clock when there is nobody here.

we will practically pass the items to-night, and we will agree not to discuss them over again unless the report contains something that makes it necessary to do so. I am sure we are most anxious to go on; but I do not think it would be proper to be placed in the position of having passed all these items without seeing the report.

It is almost six o'clock, but I would like to occupy two or three minutes to say a word in favour of the permanent schools which my hon. friend has attacked, it seems to me. with rather undue severity. As a friend of the active militia, I take a second place to no one; but I believe that the permanent force also

is a most useful force. While it may be improved, and I believe it will be in the future, it is giving valuable service to this country. Last session the minister introduced a pension system which will have the effect of inducing better men to enter the permanent force, because ineir old age is provided for. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) spoke of the incompetence of those men in South Africa for active warfare. I think that if that war has demonstrated anything, it has demonstrated this, that war alone is the test of a soldier's efficiency. A man may be trained ever so well, and may yet show in the field of battle an incompetence for war. But among the officers who distinguished themselves in South Africa were Colonel Otter, Colonel Buchan, Colonel Lessard and Colonel Evans, every one of them permanent officers.
And Colonel Durie.
And Colonel Durie-I have not time to mention them all.
He is not a permanent officer.

These men did good service in South Africa. The hon. member for Victoria did extremely good work there too-I have heard that from many men-and he is not a permanent officer. I wish to pay him that tribute. 1 have been told that there was no more efficient free lance in South Africa than Col. Hughes. My hon. friend left the impression on the mind of the House that these permanent schools were places where young men learned bad habits-where they spent a great deal of time in drinking. I have had three courses at Stanley Barracks in Toronto, and I can assure my hon. friend that we had no time for hard drinking, even if we had the inclination, which we had not; and the rule against treating in the ante-room was rigidly enforced. There may be occasionally a young man who, in the words of Kipling, sometimes ' goes wide a bit;' but that is not the fault of the place, but only the result of youth and foolishness.

speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon. M. E. Bernier).

speechtext: How does the minister grant the regular increases ? Does the clerk get his increase on the recommendation of the chief ?
The increase is regulated or fixed by Order in Council, five per cent on their minimum salary.	[DOT]
Has the statutory increase been granted to every member of the staff ?
Yes.
There are no exceptions, granted to all ?
No exceptions.
Does that item include inspectors of coal oil ?
We have no special officer of that class. The ordinary officials are performing the duties of inspecting coal oil.
I wished to know if the inspector of coal oil at Fort William comes under this head.
I may state to the hon. gentleman that we have no special inspector of coal oil. Our regular officers of the excise perform these duties.
Who inspected the coal oil last summer coming into Fort William from the United States ?
The collector of customs at Port Arthur.
Has there been any complaint made to the department regarding that coal oil.

Yes, we have had complaints.
Mi-. BOYD. Who did you find was to blame in regard to it ?
We have had some complaints, and we are now investigating them.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that there is a matter that has caused widespread dissatisfaction throughout Manitoba and the North-west. During the last season there came into that country from the United States quantities of coal oil that was simply abominable. It was distributed throughout Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and in many cases it was found so unfit for use that it was thrown away, or destroyed. Now, I believe and the people of that country believe, that this government, and the department who has charge of it, are directly responsible for the admission

of that coal oil. We know that since this government took charge of the affairs of this country they have made alterations in the coal oil inspection, they have made regulations in regard to importation of coal oil by permitting it to come into this country in tank vessels, and by certain other changes they have put the whole of the coal oil business into the hands of the American or Standard Oil Company. That is pretty well established throughout Canada at the present time. The coal oil that 1 speak of is brought in by that company,_and as I say, was distributed throughout the west. Certain complaints were made, in fact the whole press of that country was ringing with complaints about that oil, I may say from Calgary to the Red river. At first the Liberal press claimed that the government were in no way responsible for it, and the manager of the Standard Oil Company explained it in a way, saying that they had brought it in in large quantities, had stored it in large tanks, and that by reason of storing it in these large tanks and drawing it from the top or the bottom, I forget which, a certain sediment had formed in it, and in consequence the oil turned out to be bad. But he claimed they were not to blame, that they were looking into it, and were going to ascertain what bad oil was in the country and have it returned. But as I say, the Liberal press of the country claimed the department was in no way responsible. Afterwards, however, I understand that the department began to recognize their responsibility, and directed their officers to inquire into it and ascertain if an inferior oil was being sold. They were to examine the oil that was being offered for sale after giviug the company, as we believe, ample time to remove the inferior oil from the hands of the merchants. Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a very serious state of affairs, and I expect that the minister is prepared to give us a full explanation.

I may state to the hon. member that there are two ways by which that oil is inspected. When it is Canadian oil it is inspected at the refinery ; when it is imported it is inspected by the customs officer. We had some complaints made during the fall. We ordered an analysis made of oil from Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and after such analysis it was found that this Oil was in conformity with the law as it stands now, and as it has stood for the last eight or ten years. Afterwards we had another complaint, and we ordered a collection of samples to be made in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and that oil is now being analysed by Mr. Kenrick, of Winnipeg, and we are waiting for the result of his analysis.

The minister states that samples that were examined
were found to be all right according to the law of the past ten years.
Yes.
Has the law been changed in any respect during the last ten years ?
No, not with regard to the gravity or flash of the oil.
I think the minister is mistaken. Has there not been some omission with regard to testing as to quality?
No.
Did the minister take any samples from the tanks at Fort William in consequence of this complaint ?
Yes.

Was it not known to the department that the company had taken samples of this oil, and had taken it to their headquarters at Chicago in order to ascertain if it was of inferior quality ? Is the government aware of that ?
The department is not aware of that.

Who is specially charged in Montreal with the inspection of oil ? I do not know if the minister is aware that there have been a great many complaints in all the counties surrounding Montreal in respect to the quality of the oil imported. Have these complaints reached the department ?
None from the district of Montreal.
Was there an inspector appointed specially for the inspection of oils in the district of Montreal ?
No.
Is there no inspection then of oils coming into Montreal ? There is a large consumption there.
It is inspected by the customs officer, as I have already stated. We have no special officer for that purpose. Some of the officers of my department perform that duty when required.
Have there been any analyses of these oils arriving in Montreal ?
Not since I have been in the department.

I understood the minister to say that there had been no changes made. I find the old Act reads this way :

The quantity and quality of imported naphtha or petroleum- in eao'a package should be ascertained by weighing and measuring, by the inspector.
The new Act says :
The quantity of petroleum or naphtha should be ascertained by weighing or measuring.
Nothing about quality.

I understand from the minister that the inspection by the customs officer does not cover the quality of the oil. Is there any report made to the government as to the quality of the oil imported into Montreal ?

No.
Mr. IiOYIJ. I do not think the minister has explained this matter satisfactorily to the committee. If that oil was properly inspected, as it should have been, it would have been impossible for such a large quantity to be sent broadcast over the country to be sold. It was one of the leading planks in the Liberal party, when they were asking to be returned to power that the people were charged too much for their coal oil. I remember that the present leader of the government shed tears-an hon. friend suggests that they were crocodile tears, but that is a matter of course-when lie condoled with the women of Selkirk over the enormous price they had to pay for coal oil, a necessary of life, in the long winter evenings, when better coal oil could be bought on the other side of the boundary for very much less money. We find the coal oil is the same price in Manitoba and the North-west Territories to-day as it was then. But, owing to the changes that have been made, the coal oil is not so good. There was an inspection in those days for quality as well as quantity. The government is certainly responsible for the change, and the mere fact that the coal oil comes in in small packages, or large packages, in vessels or in tank cars, does not exonerate the government in the least. And, if it is for the payment of these officers and the continuation of this system that the government are asking for this money, it is well that the public should understand it.

My department has only to comply with the law which requires that oil should be tested for its flash and gravity. As I have stated, the inspection of oil coming from the United States is made by the customs officers, while the test of the Canadian oil is made at the place where it is refined. We did not refuse to act upon the complaints that were received. As I have stated, we analyzed samples and found that they complied with the law, with regard to flash and gravity. But, the complaints having been repeated, we ordered a collection of new samples and these are now undergoing

chemical analysis. If the law is defective, the government or the department may be held responsible for the necessary changes. But I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that it would be better to await the result of the analysis before changing the law. Except for the changes that the hon. gentleman has stated, the terms are the same. The department will always be ready to hear complaints and to remedy any evils that are found to exist. As to the payment of the officers, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) is going a little too far. I have already stated that we have no special officer to inspect coal oil. That work is done by the regular excise officers. But these officers are the same men who occupied the positions before the advent to power of the present government. I do not think the criticism is fair to these gentlemen. I have been associated with them for two years, and, with a few exceptions, they have fulfilled their duties faithfully.
Do I understand that the same inspection of coal oil coming into this country in small barrels is practiced as was formerly practiced ?
Y'es, there has been no change. What the officers used to do in the past they are doing now.

In the past, when coal oil was brought in in small barrels, a stamp was put on the end of the barrel, so that the retailer selling the oil had an opportunity to understand the test that had been made. How is that arranged now ?
I understand that the law requiring a mark on the package was done away with in order that the oil might be shipped in in tank cars. The amendment was made in 1898 *or 1899.

We are asked to vote this large sum of $490,000; and I see on the next page of the estimates a vote of $122,000 for the inspection of weights, measures, gas and electric light. I understand that the immense quantity of coal oil that comes into Montreal now, for which we pay a higher price than we did before the present government came into power, and as to which there has been complaints, is left absolutely without inspection as to quality.

If I repeat myself, it is only that I may be well understood. There is no special inspection of such oil by the excise officers of the Inland Revenue Department. That inspection is made by the customs officers.
As to quantity, not as to quality, I understand,
As to the test required by law.

For the information of the minister, I wish to speak on behalf of the

section of the country I represent, but I understand that the case is common over the whole country. During the past winter, consumers of coal oil have been practically robbed by having sold to them an oil of quite inferior quality. This is a condition of affairs that has not hitherto prevailed. I do not know, and it is not material as I understand the present discussion, whether the law provides for such a case or not. The point 1 want to make is that the condition exists and that it is absolutely necessary to provide fully for that condition at this session of parliament, so that, if an effort should be made to again impose upon the public, effectual means will have been provided against that imposition.

I do not pretend to say that the experience of the past year or two will not make necessary changes in the law. But my hon. friend must await, as I do, the result of the analysis that is now going on, and which, I claim, will be completed in time to enable us to change the law if it is found necessary. We have done what we thought was our duty to do, and the government cannot be held responsible for the importation of that oil. All we have to do is to comply with the law as it is. If it is proven that the law is insufficient, then it will be the duty of the government to change it in order to remedy these evils.
What qualifications has the officer at Fort William to inspect oil ?
He is not an officer of my department, but a customs officer. I cannot vouch for his qualifications. I do not know the gentleman who has charge of that duty.

Might I take a position to some extent opposed to the minister when he says that we must await the result of the analysis before we change the law ? I say the analysis which the consumers of coal oil have been compelled to make during the last six months is sufficient evidence that action is required. If the law as it is now does not cover the case, then it should-I will go so far as to say that it must-be made to cover that case for the future, irrespective of any chemical analysis. The analysis may be necessary to decide .iust exactly the terms in which the law should provide for the future, but it is clear either that the law has not been maintained or that it does not properly provide for the protection of the public.

I would like to know what this law is. For it seems to me that under this government the Standard Oil Company has been allowed to import oil in tank steamers, and we have been deprived of the certificate which was on the package which formerly was necessary. Under the law, the Department of Inland Revenue has power of inspection. There is nothing in 37
the law to prevent the Department of Inland Revenue from inspecting coal oil coming in without any mark as to quality. And surely it is impossible, I do not say for the minister, but for the officers of the department, to ignore the fact that there have been complaints. Complaints are rife throughout the country-I know they exist in my own section-as to the great deterioration of the quality of the oil imported for three or four years past. This is all the more remarkable as there has been an increase in the prices.

When the law was changed in 1899 it was at the request of the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories who wanted to have the price of oil reduced. In order to reach that end the law was changed and it was made permissible to carry coal oil in large tanks to be distributed at a cheaper rate. But, in regard to the inspection of oil, there was no change and the only way to deal with the matter that I see at the present moment is that when the analysis is made, if anything is wrong, or if any other oil or mixture enters into the oil which is imported or sold, then, we might change the law, or enact a law, in order to have a closer inspection. But, Just now, we cannot exceed the power we have as to the test of the oil, and in that respect I understand that the law was not changed.

The hon. gentleman accounted for some of the increases that appear here by stating that there were some changes made in the inspectoral divisions. Will the hon. gentleman state where these changes were made and what is the effect of them ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) knows that we have six classes of Inland Revenue divisions. When the business of a division which belongs to, say, class 4, is such as to entitle that division to be changed from the 4th to the 3rd, or 2nd class, the salaries of the officers of the division are thereby Increased according to a certain schedule of salaries of collectors, deputy collectors, excise men and clerks.
Were not some changes made in the Windsor division within the last few months ?
No.
No changes ?
Not in regard to a change in the classification of that division.

I mean in the personnel.
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE, There were changes in the personnel of the staff.
Will the hon. gentleman state what the changes were ?

Perhaps my hon. friend will give me another opportunity. There are changes contemplated and suggested, but I am not opeu now to say what these are because they require the signature of His Excellency. In a week, perhaps sooner, I will be in a position to state to the hon. gentleman what these changes are.
Have there been any changes yet made in the personnel of the staff ?
None, except the superannuation of Mr. Gow.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will state the reason for superannuating Mr. Gow ?
He is 70 years of age and he, himself, asked for his superannuation.
His age is his crime, 1 suppose?
We were very anxious to retain his services, but, lie himself pressed us to grant him superannuation.

I fancy that there are not many men pressing for superannuation. I fancy that when we look over the records, and if the newspapers are to be credited, we will find that hon. gentlemen are dropping heads into the basket either by superannuation or dismissal. I suppose Mr. Gow did not want to go to the guillotine and he asked, rather than suffer a worse fate, to be superannuated ? Was that the case with this gentleman ?

I can tell the hon. gentleman that he had better rely on what I say and not on the newspapers. I am perfect ly sure of what I say. He asked for his superannuation and we granted his request. He pressed us because he was sick as the hon. gentleman must know and he could no longer fulfil the duties of his office.
Was there any marked increase in the business of that division ?
No marked increase for a year or two past, except perhaps that caused by the establishment of one or two tobacco manufactories.

I would like to know a little more in regard to this question of coal oil. I find on looking over the coal oil inspection matter that the date referred to by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) regarding the complaints was between the 20th and 30th of November. It seems that it took

from that time until about the 24th of January before the cry which was broadcast, as has been stated by the hon. member and myself, throughout the country, could reach the ears of the department here. The papers, as I have already remarked, were full of it, and now, on the 15th March, the minister comes to this House and asks us to defer judgment until such time as the department is able to ascertain something further in regard to the complaints that have been made. There is no doubt, Mr. Chairman, about this at all. It is a scandal and there is no use in the government trying to get away from their responsibility by asking us to defer judgment, because they have had since the 24th of November last to find out about the quality of this coal oil. I would like to know the name of the man who inspected that oil and who permitted oil of that kind to come into the country. The Standard Oil Company have said that it was owing to the large tanks they stored it in, but we have learned that the same class of oil has been sold by that company to the people of North Dakota on the boundary line adjoining Manitoba, showing, beyond doubt, that the same class of oil was being supplied by that company to th* purchasers of oil in the adjoining districts. I think the least the hon. gentleman could do is to let the items stand until such time as he is able to give us more information than he has yet given us regarding this matter.

I do not think I can give more information to the hon. gentleman than I can give tonight. I have already stated that I was not aware of the complaints in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. The first intimation we had in the department that there were complaints was about six weeks ago. A sample of the oil was sent down to the department and was analyzed and in order to give satisfaction to the people who had complained we ordered our inspector at Winnipeg, Mr. Barrett, to make a collection of samples of the oil throughout Manitoba and the North-west Territories, the said samples of oil to be analyzed by Mr. Ivenrick, and we are now waiting for the result of this analysis.

Is this analysis in regard to quality of the oil ? The law does not call for a test of quality. Is it not so that the present law does not demand an analysis so far as quality is concerned ? 1 think the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) has read the old law and the new law, and as he read it, in the new law there is no tests of quality.
There was no test for quality in any law beyond a test for flash and gravity.

The hon. member for Macdonald read the old law as he

thought it appeared and it certainly called for a test of lighting quality. The hon. minister states that this law was changed at the instigation of the people of Manitoba in order that they should secure cheaper coal oil. They certainly did not get what they asked for. They are paying just as much for their oil to-day as they were before the change. I think the hon. minister is wrong in stating that there has been no change in the law so far as the test as to quality is concerned. It is because of the change that inferior oil is coming into this country. The Standard Oil Company have admitted that the quality was inferior although they say it was limited to one or two tanks that were admitted at the port of Emerson. The oil has been of the most inferior character and a great outcry has been raised through the west irrespective of politics. I may say that if the people asked for a change in the law for the sake of getting good oil at a reasonable price, they have failed in their purpose because they have got inferior oil.
May I ask the hon. minister if it is possible that oil may pass the inspection for flash and gravity and still be ferior for illuminating purposes ?
It may be.
So that the law in no way protects us as to the burning quality of the oil ?
It is the same as in the past.

It seems a remarkable thing that when oil exists for the purpose of giving illumination the question of the illuminating quality of the oil is not provided for in any test that is made. We do not care so much about the flash test, or the gravity of the oil ; what we want to know is whether it will give light when it burns. As a matter of fact, a large part of the oil that was supplied in Manitoba and the North-west Territories during the past winter would not give light and some of it would not even burn.
I actually have seen my lamp go out. It does not make any difference to us what the flash test is, or what the gravity is so long as the illuminating power of the oil is not there. I am astonished to hear the Minister of Inland Revenue say that this condition of affairs did not come to the knowledge of his department until six weeks ago. If that is the fact it is high time that the Inland Revenue staff in Manitoba and the North-west should be changed from beginning to end; from top to bottom. We want men in the employ of the Inland Revenue Department and in the other departments of the government as well, who are aware of the facts that are transpiring around them and who understand what 37*
their responsibility is to the public, as well as to the department itself. If they thick that their only business is to dra'w their salaries I would like them wakened up from that idea. The grounds on which we vote then- salaries here at any rate is, that their business is to look after the protection of the public and if they have not informed the head of the department of this condition of affairs which has been a matter of universal comment throughout Manitoba and the North-west Territories for the last five months, it seems to me they should be called sharply to account.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

Not yet. It seems that the department has no information on this matter and so we will try to supply them with some. They do not seem to know anything about it, so it is just as well to tell the minister all we know about it. I wish to ascertain if it is true, that the Standard Oil Company, now that they are permitted to import oil in tank vessels and otherwise control the oil business of this country ; is it true that they are selling their best refined oil to-day in foreign countries where they have to meet competition, and that they are passing off on the people of the North-west a quality of illuminating oil that some years ago they sold as fuel oil. That is what they are doing. They are sending their best oil to Europe to compete with the Russian oil, but as they completely control the markets of Manitoba and the North-west they are selling us their worst quality of oil, and they are allowed to do this under the inspection of the government, and with the approval of the government officers. We have shown here tonight that the people of the west have been imposed on and have been robbed in this connection.

The hon. gentleman is under the impression evidently, that there has been a change in the regulations concerning the quality of oil. The officers of the department state that there has been no Such change, and certainly I am not aware of such a change. It has not been the policy of any government, as I understand it, to determine the quality of the oil in the sense in which the word has been used here. The safeguards are against oil of a dangerous character being used. That has been the main purpose of the checks surrounding the sale of petroleum.
I do not think the Minister of Finance would say that if he had the old Act at hand, and read the clause

I have not the Act, but my hon. friend has, and if he will read it he will find it is quite consistent with what I say. I am informed that the only place where the word quality is used is with reference to the

marks on tlie barrels; that the quality and quantity shall correspond with the marks on the barrel and the marks on the barrel allude to the quantity, the specific gravity and the flash test. The essence of the whole question is, whether there has been a change in the law respecting the quality of the oil, and the officers who are well informed on the subject say there has been no change whatever, and that it was not the policy of any previous administration to determine the illuminating power of the oil. There are thousands of things sold in Canada which are not up to the standard, nor always up to sample even, but they are not in all cases inspected by the government. If a man buys an inferior article and pays a high price for it he is wronged, but that is not the fault of the government. It may be that there should be some wider law on the subject ; it may be that the illuminating power should be guaranteed ; it may be that the quality of flour and fish and various things which are inspected only iii a limited way, should be guaranteed; but whether or not that be the case, the point is that there has been no change in the law with respect to the quality of the oil.

How is it then, that bulletins are frequently issued by the Department of Inland Revenue giving the results of the examinations of such articles as pickles, butter, cheese, mustard, &c. It is possible that under the present law the power does not exist in the department to cause an inspection to be made of this illuminating oil. I understood from the Minister of Inland Revenue that that inspection had not been made once in the district of Montreal, and I understand further that he maintains that it cannot be made under the law as it at present exists. Is there a law governing the inspection of the articles which I have mentioned, but which restricts the department from inspecting coal oil ?

The articles mentioned by the hon. gentleman are articles of food, and there is a law with respect to the adulteration of food.
Mr. OSLEIt. Ret me read this clause from the old Act, and I think that you will find that it contradicts what the Minister of Finance has said :
The quantity and quality of imported petroleum so imported i'l each package shall be ascertained Ly weighing and testing by the inspector.
That does not mean that the inspection Is merely to ascertain what marks are on the package, but it says that the oil itself is to be inspected as to its quality.
I am informed that the word ' quality ' there as read in connection with another section has reference to the marks on the barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That surely cannot be the meaning of the clause.

My hon. friend has the Act there and I have not. I am assured by the officers who are supposed to know all about it, that there has been no change whatever in the Act with regard to the inspection as to the quality of the oil. It has not been the practice to do more than to ascertain that the oil was of the gravity and flash test required. Whether or not there should be the power to further inspect as to quality is a fair question for discussion.
Do I understand the Minister of Finance to say that at no time has there been a test made to determine the illuminating power of the oil ?
It has not been the practice of the department to guarantee the illuminating power of the oil, and there has been no change in the law in that respect in recent years.
Prior to the introduction of the new law, tests were made and these tests were stamped at the end of the barrel. Could the minister tell the House what these stamps indicated ?
The usual marks for quantity and the test for specific gravity and safety are on the barrel, but there is no mark certifying to the illuminating power.
In the investigation which is now going on by the department, are you testing the illuminating power of the oil ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In view of the statements made by the members from the North-west Territories and Manitoba, will the minister make a regulation or have the Act so amended as to prevent people from selling an adulterated article.

The remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Taylor), strike the nail on the head. It seems to be somewhat an academic question whether any change has been made in the regulations, or whether it is possible under the present law to remedy the defect. If it is not possible to apply the present law for the protecetion of the people in this matter, would it not be possible for this House to confer upon the government, power to apply a remedy ? With regard to many articles of merchandise, which are not subject to inspection, the public are protected by competition ; but there is not competition in coal oil in the North-west. A monopoly has control of the .whole market, and if the government cannot afford protection to the people against the poor article which without any shadow of doubt has

been fraudulently sold to them during the past few months, then they are without any protection whatever.

It seems to be very difficult for the members to understand the change which has been made in the law. Will the hon. minister be good enough to read to the House the old law and the new clause, so that the House will understand the change that has been made ?

I will have the law in a few minutes ; but in the meantime, in answer to my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor), I may say that the moment the department heard that there were complaints, we instructed our officer in Manitoba to collect samples in order to ascertain the quality of the oil, and I think it is only just and fair to await the result of that investigation, when the law, if necessary, will be amended.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend will have the result of that investigation before the House rises-in time to amend the law.
Yes, within a couple of weeks.

I wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that it was about three months after the complaints commenced that we are told the department took action. The manager of the Standard Dil Company stated in an interview with the iiress that instructions had been given by their company to withdraw all the inferior oil. Now, the government proposes to take samples of the oil offered for sale after giving the company, as it would seem, plenty of time to withdraw all the inferior oil from the market. I asked the minister to-night if samples were taken from the tanks, and he answered me no. That shows the untenable position the government occupy in this matter.
I would like to ask the minister how long it is since the investigation began, who conducted it, and how soon it is expected to be ended and the report handed in ?

I have already stated that about six weeks ago we received some complaints. Immediately we ordered that a sample of the oil be sent to the department. A sample was sent. We heard something further about the matter, and we immediately instructed our officer in Winnipeg, Mr. Barrett, to collect samples, and have an analysis made by Mr. Kenrick. Under these circumstances, I think it would not be fair to the officers of the department to act as if they had not done their duty. I regret that the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) says that these officers should be dismissed. What would be the use of dismissing them and replacing them with men Mr. MONK.
of less experience, who would be in the same position, that is, prevented from doing what my hon. friend asks us to do, bearing in mind that the law does not permit us to go any further at present.

The minister states that it is only right that we should await the report of this investigation before we have any amendment made to the Act.
I do not think that is necessary at all. That is equivalent to saying that he does not know whether there has been spurious oil sent into the country or not. Surely it is not a spurious agitation which has taken place all over the North-west. The Standard Oil Company themselves admit that they have sent in inferior oil. What better proof do you want than that ? They say only a limited quantity was sent in ; but I think they underestimate the quantity. The oil sent in during the last few months lias been spurious without any doubt, and I think it is not necessary to await the report of this investigation before amending tlie Act. The Act should be amended right away, without waiting for the report of Mr. Barrett or any one else, because it has been stated here by members on both sides of the House that the oil is inferior in illuminating power.

I think my hon. friend has misunderstood me. I have positively stated that we expect the report of the analysis within two weeks, and then we shall be ready to take action. I think the House will be still sitting at that time, and we shall have ample time to change the law, if it is found necessary. With regard to these complaints in the North-west, there was no complaint made except at the time I have already stated. It may be that the hon. gentlemen who represent Manitoba and the Territories may have heard more than I heard myself ; but that is no fault of the department, and we acted as soon as any complaint reached us, which was about six weeks ago.
I would like to ask tlie minister if the Act, Chapter 102 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1886. ' an Act for the Inspection of Petroleum,' has been changed?
Yes, it has been.

If it has been changed, it can only have been changed in such a manner as to extend the powers of inspection of the department. I have not read tlie Act over with attention, but I have no doubt that the fire test has not been changed.
The expression fire test or burning means the ignition and continuous burning ot any fluid hereinafter referred to, on1 the application of a light or spark under regulations established by this Act.
That has not been changed, and with such a statutory condition as that, there is no

doubt that the department itself possesses power to make regulations for the naming of an inspector to remedy the evil mentioned by the hon. members from the Northwest. If that is the case, then the department is at fault, and the suggestion made by one of the hon. minister's own friends, that the whole staff ought to be dismissed, including the head-because he said from top to bottom-should be carried out.

It seems from the statements made by the minister so far that action on the part of the government depends on the report that may be made by the officers after their investigation of certain samples which they have collected. If it should turn out, however, as the hon. member from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) suggested, that the officers procured samples of good oil, then we have to take it that the department will feel justified in not taking any action at all. It seems to me that the evidence given by several members on the floor of the House to-night should be sufficient for the department. I can give the hon. minister my own word, from painful personal experience, as to the very bad character of some of the coal oil that was sold in the North-west during the last few months. I have attempted to read newspapers by lamp light produced by some of this oil, and it was almost totally impossible to do so. I believe the stuff would freeze readily at zero, and I believe that more profanity has been caused in western Canada by this bad oil during the last few months than was caused even by the grain blockade we were talking about on Monday. I know that nothing less will satisfy the people of that country than a definite statement by the government that they intend to protect the public in this matter. As I have said, the coal oil trade there is in the hands of a monopoly ; there is no competition to protect the people, and the conditions during the past season have shown the necessity for the inspection going farther than it has gone, so that the purchaser may know that the article he buys will give the expected light.

I think that if the minister had complied with the request made to him to read the clause, as to the inspection under the old Act, and the new clause we might have been saved some time and discussion. Is the minister prepared to do that now ? If the two Acts are as stated in the paper that has been read from on this side, then, it is quite clear that the old Act was sufficient for the purpose. When you are testing illuminating oil, I presume the first thing is to test its illuminating qualities.
There is another paragraph in the clause.

That is the reason that I am asking that the old section shall be read as well as the new one. If the old section is Mr. MONK,
as quoted on this side, it seems sufficient, and the new clause is not sufficient for the purpose.

That there may be no misapprehension in the mind of any hon. member, I will read the whole of section 7 :
The quantity and quality of imported petroleum or nap'nt'ia in each package shall be ascertained by weighing and testing by the inspector, and the allowance of the tare of the package shall be in accordance with the departmental regulation in that behalf.
And section 14 provides :
Every refiner, manufacturer or importer of petroleum or naphtha, and every person who deals in or keep? or offers any petroleum or naphtha for sale shall be responsible as to its quality and as to the quantity contained in each package that the same shall not be inferior to the quality uor less than the quantity designated by the marks and descriptions then on the packages in which it is contained. All of which marks and descriptions the person in whose possession it is shall maintain in a perfectly legible state.
The last part was amended.
Will the hon. minister read the last part in section 7 after the word ' inspector ' ?

I will read it all :
The quantity and quality of imported petroleum or naphtha in each package shall be ascer-ta'ned by weighing and testing by the inspector, and the allowance for the tare of the package shall be in accordance with the departmental regulations in that behalf.
What is the departmental regulations in that behalf ?
It is the regulation which was in force before the law was amended.
Can the hon. minister tell us what they were ?
It was that it should be inspected by weighing and testing by the instruments that were described in the regulation.

It seems to me that the request made by some hon. gentleman from the North-west that this matter should be allowed to stand until we have an opportunity to look further into the question is a reasonable one. In view of the difficulty we have had in ascertaining what the law is, I think we ought to be granted that grace.

I do not see how allowing the item to stand can affect the general question which has been raised as to the desirability of a better inspection law. That is a fair question for discussion, but I do not see how it can be affected by this item or how a good purpose can be saved by having the item stand.

The question is not so much what the law is, as it is whether the department has been at fault in, not making a proper inspection in that, in inspecting illuminating oil, the one point they did not inspect was its illuminating quality. Before this money is voted for the department, we want to see whether the department is at fault or not.

The hon. minister has made a very positive statement-and I believe that there is no dispute about the fact-that there has never been an inspection of that particular character. The question is somewhat technical, and I do not offer any opinion of my own upon it. But I am informed by those who ought to know that the marks upon the package showing the gravity and the flash test are enough to enable those who understand these matters to work out the illuminating power. But, if the illuminating power does not result, there is some defect somewhere.
The hon. minister seems to think that because a thing was never done before complaint was made, that is a reason why it should not be done after complaint has been made.
Not at all.

That is the result of the hon. gentleman's argument. I do not understand that, in times past, the people of the North-west have had oil which would not burn or would not give light. A few mouths ago they got that kind of oil and complaints were made. And, those complaints having been made, the department should have ascertained the grounds for them.

I think it would be of no use to have the item stand. For, if it takes two weeks before we can ascertain what kind of oil is used in the North-west, the House will have uo opportunity of discussing this question any more. I have already stated that, since the law was first enacted that law was found workable. About six weeks ago we heard complaints. Were we derelict in our duty ? No, we acted as soon as we heard those complaints. They may have reached members of this House from the North-west before they reached us. 1 do not say those hon. gentlemen were derelict in their duty, but I do say that if we had been sooner informed of their complaints we could have taken action sooner. But, the moment we were informed that complaints were made in the North-west, we took action and had samples sent here to be tested, and I immediately ordered that samples should be collected for analysis. How can we change the law if we do not know in what sense it should be changed ? It is very well for these gentlemen to say- and I do not say that their information is
inaccurate-that the oil sold is of inferior quality, but we want to have the evidence by way of a more strict inspection. I have already said, and I repeat, that, as soon as we see that a change in that law is necessary in order to protect the people in Manitoba and the North-west, with the assistance of the hon. gentlemen from the North-west, we will make the law to meet the case and give satisfaction to the people. I cannot say more. I have no objection to the discussion of the item. But I regret that, not being master of the English language,
I do not seem to make myself well understood. If I cannot convince my hon. friends by using their language, perhaps I shall be obliged to use my native French.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister assured us that if he ascertained that it is necessary, he will have the law amended. But I thiulc he went just a little too far when he said that the law would be so amended as to give the people satisfaction. That I do not think he can do, because our friends from the North-west say just what we on this side said in 1897. I spoke pretty strongly on that myself. When the government came down with a Bill to amend the law as it then stood permitting the Standard Oil Company to come into this country with their tank vessels and tank ships, we opposed it; and when a gentleman from that side of the House who was interested in the Canadian oil industry-I refer to the late Judge Lister-got up and threatened to oppose the government if they went on with the legislation, it was dropped. I said then that the Standard Oil Company were just getting what they had paid for, because they had made a large contribution to the election fund in 1890.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You ought to know.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: To my hon. friends opposite, who promised the legislation. However, the government withdrew the measure that year. By the next year the late Judge Lister had been removed to the bench, he was not in the House to make any opposition, and then the government came down and carried out the bargain they had made with the Standard Oil Company previous to the election. They introduced and put through that Bill that we said would give the monopoly that our friends in the Northwest say now they have got. They got just what the government had bargained for. We told them when they changed that law and let the Standard Oil Company into this country, that it would drive out the Canadian industry, and that they would get control of our market. They have got it, and they are getting now just what they bargained for when this government sold the country to the Standard Oil Company.

Do I understand the minister to say that under the old system of in-

spection and stamping on the end of the barrel, one of those stamps indicated the quantity of oil in the barrel ?
Yes.

Under the old system, then, all the coal oil that was brought in from the United States to Canada came in small barrels holding about 40 gallons. On the end of each barrel were these stamps, one stamp indicating the quantity of oil contained in the barrel. As I understand now, since the change has been made, most of the oil coming in from the United States comes in large tanks. For illustration, it comes Into the city of Toronto in large tanks. There are many towns within a radius of 50 miles of Toronto where there is no distributing tanks going through the town. When these towns get their oil which is sent from Toronto by the Standard Oil Company In small barrels, the same kind of barrels as was used before the change in the law, will the minister be good enough to tell us what system of inspection they now have, so that the retail merchants may know the quantity of oil contained in the barrel that he now gets under the new regulations ?

On one point the hon. gentleman is mistaken, in saying that prior to that change in the law till oil was brought in in barrels. The oil was brought in under the old system in tank cars as well as in barrels, but not in tank steamers. There were other minor matters, but the material change in the law was to the effect that if you could bring in oil in tank ears in the western part of the Dominion, you might be allowed to bring it in in tank ships in the eastern part of the Dominion.
