The effect was that every gallon of oil used in the western part of the province of Ontario was brought in in small barrels.
No, it was brought in in tank cars, largely.
Brought in in tank cars prior to the change of the law in 1899 ?
It was brought in in tank ears in large quantities, and was only put in barrels after it was imported into the country.
There was an inspection, then, and the inspection was stamped upon the end of the barrel, and now there is no inspection. That is the change, is it ?
There is an inspection, but it is not stamped.
Why is it not stamped ?

I am not an expert in coal oil, but I have just read Mr. BLAIN.
the statute, and here is the conclusion to which I have come with respect to the requirements of the statute. Under the old system all coal oil was brought into the country either in small packages, in barrels, or it was brought in in tank cars. The oil brought in in tank cars, before it could be sold, had to be barrelled. When barrelled it was inspected, and the result of the inspection with respect to the flash test and the gravity was stamped on the end of the barrel. Under the new law which is in force since 1899, oil may be imported in tank cars, or in.barrels, and in tank ships. The difference between the old law and the present law is that, instead of insisting upon the oil being barrelled before it is offered for sale, it is now permissible to sell the oil by the gallon from the tank car, or from the tank ship, or from the barrel. The inspection is made, but the result of the inspection is not stamped on the barrel. That is the difference, as I understand it, reading the two statutes.
Mr: BORDEN (Halifax). I am not familiar with the statute, but it seems to me a rather singular provision that there should be an inspection of the oil in barrels, and that the result should not be stamped upon the barrel.
The inspection would be made before the oil is put in the barrel.

But here you have a barrel containing a certain measure-able article that has undergone inspection. I am not at all suggesting that the Minister of Justice was wrong about it, but merely suggesting that it seems to me a remarkable provision that there should be an inspection, and that the public should not be made aware, by some mark upon the package containing the article, that there has been an inspection and what the results are. I do not know when such a measure passed the House, but I am bound to say I do not think it is a very wise provision of this legislature or of any other legislature, to have an inspection without announcing the result upon the package.
The inspection we have now is absolutely the same inspection as that which was in force previous to 1899-the one inspection, both as to dash test and gravity.
There is a difference in this respect, that formerly the result was on the package and now it is not.

Yes, we have to assume that to be the case, that there is no information conveyed to the public in respect to the result of the inspection. Of course the inspection has taken place in order to ensure the safety of the public. The inspection by the customs official is ample for the purpose.

It is very distressing to liear the complaints from the North-west regarding coal oil, and I am sure we are all extremely sorry that they are in the dark up there. I would suggest that the western members move down to Ontario where we have good coal oil. I happen to be a dealer in coal oil, among other things, and can vouch for the quality of the oil that is delivered in Ontario. We used to buy it altogether for retail use in barrels, now It is delivered in tanks, and we have to take the word of the wholesale dealer who sells it to us. His wagon comes around to our shops, and he fills up our tank, and we suppose it to be of the proper gravity, and flash, and everything of proper quality. We have no complaints regarding it. Our people are well satisfied with regard to the quality of the coal oil ; and I think in that respect, at any rate, the matter is quite satisfactory to the people of Ontario. I can well understand though that if a dealer chose to be dishonest, if he took coal oil from the tank and put it in the barrel without having it properly marked by an inspector, there might be an invasion of the law there. I rose to say that the present mode of delivery of coal oil In Ontario is quite satisfactory to the- dealers and to the public.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that now the system is that tank wagons come around and deliver the coal oil ?

Yes, they come around our way.
Mr. BLAIN The hon. member lives at Port Perry ; does the tank call at his town?
Yes.
And at other towns in the riding of South Ontario ?
Yes.
All the other towns ?
I do not know that.

All I have to say is that the town in which I live Is very much larger' In population than Port Perry It is marvellous how much these hon. gentlemen know about population, and how little about coal oil. Although the town of Brampton where I live has a very much larger population than Port Perry, every gallon of oil sold in that town comes in in barrels the same as it did for the last 20 years.
You are behind the age.

The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) knows as much about coal oil as he does about binder twine. I had occasion to hear his observations on binder twine a few weeks ago and I think it would enlighten the House very much if he would repeat his discourse upon that very important subject before the hon. members of this
House. There seems to be some fault found with the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue and with the department because coal oil is not tested for its illuminating qualities. It is well understood that the quality of oil depends upon two conditions, first, on its specific gravity, and second, on the flash test. Upon the specific gravity depends the illuminating quality of the oil and on the flash test depeuds safety from explosion. When you have these two tests, as was mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), you certainly have an assurance of the illuminating quality of the oil, because, having the specific gravity and flash test, you will find in these the illuminating qualities of - the oil. I may say that the test of Canadian oil as to specific gravity is 791 as compared with water at 1,000, while the test of American oil is, for its specific gravity, 784 as compared with 1,000 of water.
May I ask the hon. member (Mr. Campbell) what he is reading from ?
What does it matter to you ?
I ask the hon. gentleman to state what he is reading from ?
Are you prepared to state that what I am reading is not correct ?
I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that we have a right to know what the hon. gentleman is reading from ?
I am reading from notes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think an hon. gentleman is allowed to read from the notes he has before him without having to tell the committee what he is reading, just as any hon. gentleman can read the notes which he has prepared containing any figures that he has put down, and therefore, if he says these figures are before him in the form of notes, he has a perfect right to read them.
Mr. Chairman, it is not the rule of the House ?
Order, order.
I was interrupted

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No hon. gentleman can be interrupted against his will.
He may rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

I am only making these statements to show that the best samples of Canadian oil are superior to those of American oil at the present time. There has been a very great improvement in the quality of oil in the last few years and now the best quality of Canadian oil is equal to

and better than the best quality of American oil. It may be that there was poor oil sent into the North-west Territories.
It was not Canadian oil at all.

I am not prepared to say whether it was Canadian or American oil, but I am sure the position taken by the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue ought to satisfy the committee, inasmuch as he has now under investigation the complaints that were made to his department and as he assures the committee that within two weeks the result of this investigation will be known and that upon the result being known action will be taken. Surely, to my mind, that ought to satisfy the committee that the department is alive to its duty and has the interest of the public at heart.
I did not quite understand the hon. gentleman's figures in respect to the flash test, &e. Would he be good enough to repeat them again to the committee ?
I gave you a comparison as between Canadian and American oils.
It is then in respect to the flash test ?
The specific gravity.
Oh, the specific gravity. I understood the hon. gentlemiTh to say that he referred to the illuminating qualities of the oil. Was that correct ?
On the specific gravity depends the illuminating quality of the oil.

Then, I understood him correct^. Now the hon. gentleman tells the committee that the specific gravity that was formerly stamped on the end of'the barrel indicated the illuminating quality of the oil. The hon. Minister of Finance has told the committee that there never was any inspection in respect to the illuminating quality of the oil.
I did not say anything of the sort.
What did the hon. gentleman say ?

I did not say that the illuminating power of the oil, in these terms, was stamped on the barrel, but I did say that when you get specific gravity and the flash test both correctly, I was informed that they produce the illuminating power,and that any one who understood it might have indicated to him the illuminating power of the oil, but there was no specific mark in these terms that the illuminating power of the oil was so much. It had to be deduced from these figures, as I have been informed.

The fact is that at this present time, under the new regulations, there Mr. CAMPBELL.
is no test for the reason that there is nothing stamped on the end of the barrel. The changed regulations do not give an opportunity for the dealer or the consumer to know anything at all of the illuminating quality of the oil. The hon. member for West York has been good enough to read myself a lecture in respect to binder twine. I wish he would be good enough to read the House a lecture in respect to counting ballots of voters who voted four or five times in his last election. I was delighted with his remarks in his county in his recent election in respect to what an ardent protectionist he was, and with his promise that the minute he reached the House he would enter a complaint against the government for their failure to give more protection and that he would ask them to put the tariff up higher.
I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) where that was ?

I do not wonder that the hon. gentleman asks that question, because he changes his policy so quickly that he does not remember. It depends entirely on where he made the statement, as to what the statement would be. We understand that very well. He was a free trader at one time and now he is a high protectionist.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As each hon. member has departed from the rules of order and as each has had his way, I hope both will be good enough to come now to the consideration of the item under discussion.
It would be just as well to stop it at the beginning and not at this juncture.

I understood two hon. members to say, the hon. Minister of Finance, and the hon. member for West York, as with authority, that the flash test ensured safety and the specific gravity ensured illuminating power, or if I am not stating it correctly, that the two tests together, the flash test and the specific gravity test, ensured illuminating power. Am I right ?
I did not state it as on authority. I said I was informed.

1 am very sorry, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Campbell) that you have been asked to take the chair at this moment because I was left in a very painful state of uncertainty.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) read carefully from a paper, and even though he would not disclose his authority, the statement was a very important one. I remember when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) held a very different view as to the quality of Canadian coal oil. He told us to-night that the specific gravity and the flash test of the Canadian oil was much higher than that of the American oil and that therefore Canadian oil was better. It is not very long since the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) went about the country contending that the American oil was infinitely superior to the Canadian oil, that our people were slaves paying tribute to the oil kings of Canada and that the duty should be taken off oil. I am not quite sure that he did not even carry a gallon of coal oil in his hand to demonstrate his contention. Well, it is a good thing if the hon. gentleman has been converted, and we are glad to know now from him that the American oil was never as good as Canadian oil, and that he was all wrong about that in the past. Whether the law has been changed or not, enough has been said here to-night to warrant this matter receiving the serious attention of the government. I am glad to hear from the Minister of Inland Revenue that it is the intention of the government after full inquiry to see that no inferior oil is put on the market so far as it is possible for the department to guard against it.
I have already given that assurance.

I understood the hon. member (Mr. Blain) to argue that the oil which was supplied in Western Ontario came in in small barrels as it formerly did. Although the town of Brampton may be in darkness to the extent of receiving oil in barrels at the present day, it is a fact that generally throughout Western Ontario, the oil is delivered in tank wagons from tank supply centres. I cannot speak for the consumers, because I do not use oil myself, but so far as the retail dealers are concerned in the counties of Huron and Bruce with which I am most familiar, they endorse very cordially the present system and speak of the law as being thoroughly satisfactory.
Would the minister inform the House what flash light specific gravity means in respect to illuminating quality. Surely the minister in charge of the department should understand that.
That has been asked a dozen times.
Some hon. gentleman says that question has been asked a dozen times and I agree ; but the point is that we have not had an answer to the question.

I must confess that I have not very extensive practical knowledge on the question of coal oil, and even my theories do not go very far. When I took charge of the department a certain law had been in force for eight years, and that law has not been altered since with regard to the quality of the oil. Let that be well understood. I may know a great many other things, but I cannot speak with ' connaissance de cause ' in regard to the quality of oil. What I have said, I repeat now, and that is, that after an experience of eight or ten years under different governments, if we find that the law is not sufficient to protect the public then we are prepared to change or amend the law-in that respect. I think that should be sufficient. It is not to be expected from me that I should enter into a scientific discussion of the quality or the purity of coal oil; but if I be in default on that I perhaps will have some one to teach me. Even if I have to repeat myself ten times. I think it is sufficient for the House that I should say that I took the law as it was ; the law which was operated by the same officer for ten years, and the very moment that we perceived that under the existing law we could not give satisfaction to the public, we took means to ascertain to what extent the public are suffering and we are prepared to remedy the defect. I cannot say more.
A very large quantity of American oil comes to Toronto for distribution in Ontario. Would the minister tell us who inspects that oil ?
AVhen it is imported to this country it is inspected by the customs officer, and when it is manufactured in Canada it is inspected by the inland revenue officer.

AVhen is it inspected ?
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE-When it crosses the frontier I suppose.
Is there a stamp put on, the tank ?
No.

Do not the Minister of Finance, as well as the Minister of Inland Revenue, think that it is a defect in the legislation that there should be that Inspection without any mark on the package to indicate tlfat there has been inspection and the result of the inspection? I am not sufficiently familar to the trade to know the details, but looking at the question in a general way it seems to me that the legislation is defective in that respect.

The oil is imported in large packages and does not reach the consumer in that state. Though you put a stamp on the tank car it would be of very little value to the consumer, for he never gets it in a tank car. There is a heavy penalty on any person who sells coal oil in Canada which has not been inspected in the manner prescribed, and that is the protection which the public enjoys. I have been informed that until this recent matter cropped up in the North-west, there has been no complaint sent to the department.

How would it be possible to show under such a system, that any particular barrel of coal oil has or has not been inspected. If you mark the tank when you inspect it, and indicate the result of the inspection, then when that tank is emptied into barrels the proper officer could mark the barrels. It seems to me such a provision would afford better protection.
What will happen to the man who buys a gallon ?

I am speaking of the process until you get to the retail dealer. Of course every gallon measure cannot be inspected. My hon. friend (Mr. McCarthy) will see that an objection of that kind is absurd.
Mr.. MCCARTHY. My objection is not at all factious. I simply recall the fact that it is the consumer that causes all the trouble about the inferior oil.

I am speaking of the inspection for the man who sells, and you must have marks of inspection on the packages so that the person who buys will have something to rely upon. It would be extremely difficult under the present system to prove that a single barrel of coal oil which bears no marks had been inspected.

There is something in that, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) will see that he would have to follow It out down to the last gallon. The oil which is imported in tank cars or in tank ships does not always pass Into barrels. There are large standing tanks in certain places into which it is Mr. BLAIN.
passed, and then it is passed out again into other vessels. I am told that when oil is sold from a tank wagon which is the practice in western Ontario, a standard can is used which is of certified size and therefore there is protection as to quantity. However, the theory of the law is that any coal oil sold here shall not be unsafe." Of course if there is defective inspection as it has been suggested, that is another matter, but the theory of the law is that there shall be effective inspection in regard to what the law prescribes. If the oil be found on sale in Canada, the presumption is, in the absence of anything to the contrary, that it is safe and of the quality required by law; and I am afraid, though I can see the criticism which my hon. friend has applied to a particular case, that you have to risk the quality of the oil as you have that of any other- article of sale, when it comes up to the requirements of the law as to the flash test and the specific gravity.
May I ask the minister if tank cars are allowed to come into every town in the province of Ontario ?

Yes, at every port or out-port of entry in Canada.
Mr.- BOYD. I would like to ask the minister, in case the report of his officers should be that the oil they have taken for inspection from the several merchants in Manitoba is good, whether he will take any action with regard to this matter ?

It will be within two weeks, the minister says, when that report will be before the House. If we were to-night to introduce a Bill to amend the Inland Revenue Act in that respect, we would not have it enacted within two weeks.
That is not the question I asked at all.

Allow me. If the attention of the House be drawn to a defect in any law, the members of the government are bound to consider it and provide a remedy ; and while this analysis will be one element in the case, even if on other evidence it can be shown that the law is defective, the government will be bound to provide a remedy.
The question I asked was whether any action would be taken if the report of the officers was that the oil was good.
It is time enough to consider that when we have the evidence before us.

The evidence given by the members from the North-west proves conclusively that bad oil was sold through that country. There is no question about it, and I have stated upon the floor of this House that the agent of the Standard Oil

Company himself admitted that the oil was had, and that they were withdrawing it from sale ; and about a month or six weeks after that an order was issued by the Department of Inland Revenue instructing their officers to inspect oil offered for sale. They are not likely to find any thing wrong with the oil offered for sale now.

I understand that the oil must come up to a certain test, whether it is in tanks or in barrels ; and if it comes up to this test, it makes no difference whether the stamp is on the barrel or not. It comes to a town in a car tank, and is pumped from that into a wagon tank carrying 200 or 300 gallons, and this is taken to the stores and is delivered to the dealers in 5-gallon or 10-gallon tanks belonging to them. I cannot see how the oil could get into the North-west without being properly inspected. It may have been that after crossing the border a dishonest dealer put water into it and then sold it to the farmers.
I understand that the law to-day is as it always has been; but the usage is different, the oil being taken to the dealers in tank wagons instead of in barrels.

The hon. gentleman is not right in supposing that the oil is subject to any test on crossing the border. I have the tariff item before me, and in it no test is provided for. The Minister of Inland Revenue stated that the customs collector inspected the oil. There is no evidence of that in the tariff ; he only collects the duty on the number of gallons brought in.

I may state that I myself have purchased oil on more than one occasion, and before I could get it delivered, it had to be inspected by the customs officer, and I got from him a certificate stating that the oil was equal to the flash and the gravity test required by law. He had an instrument to test the oil himself.

In answer to the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) I may say that according to section 16 of the Act, all imported oils must be inspected by the customs officer at the port of entry designated by the Governor in Council.
Will the minister give us a list of the ports in the province of Ontario that are so designated ?
Every port where there is a customs officer.

I would like the hon. minister to answer the question I put to him, whether he is going to take action on the report of his officers or on the evidence brought before this House by the members from the North-west ?

I do not understand how it is possible to trace a quantity of oil which proves not to be up to the test,
and which may cause loss of life-to trace it to the proper officer and punish him for his neglect in not making a proper test.
Is that not an incident of the modern method of carrying on the oil business ?

I dare say it may be, if you call this the modern method ; but I do not know that that is a very conclusive answer to what I am suggesting to the committee. I do not suppose that my hon. friend from Westmoreland, if he happened to be blown through the roof, and came down minus an arm or a leg, would imagine that that was a satisfactory answer when he brought an action against the inspector. Of course, my hon. friend is very philosophic in regard to others, but I desire to make a personal application of the matter to himself. It seems to me that if we have an inspection, we should have such safeguards as to enable us to fix the responsibility for non-inspection dn the officers of this government.

Granting that that is the question, is it not almost inevitable ? It would be the same if it were a case of inspection of food, a man having been poisoned. It would be no great comfort to him to know that there had been inspection, which had been evaded. Yet, the inspection of food is on the whole, a good thing; and so the inspection of oil, on the whole, is a good thing. Each, in the main, works out its purpose, but there may be instances of failure, as is alleged in this case.

But the hon. minister does not understand my point. When you had a system of compulsory inspection of fish in Nova Scotia-it is not compulsory now-when a dealer bought a barrel of fish, he had the stamp of the officer upon it. The person who bought it had a remedy against the officer, if the fish was not up to the standard. But that is a circumstance which seems wanting here. I am not prepared to say that it cannot be overcome, but I suggest that it is a difficulty' that some effort ought to be made to overcome.

But, to carry that out, you would have to deal with barrels and even with smaller parcels. These would be useful checks if it is possible to carry them out, but it may not be possible. The main iiurpose of the change, not as regards inspection test or specific gravity, but as regards handling the oil, was that it could be more cheaply transported and the necessity of barrelling it would be avoided-allowing it to be carried in tank cars instead of in small parcels. It was supposed that adequate inspection at the port of entry for importeu oil, and at the refinery for Canadian oil, would amply protect the public interest.
Is oil admitted at every port in Canada ?
At *every warehousing port. At first, there was a list of ports, but it was afterwards enlarged so as to include all warehousing imports.
As I understand it, there is an inspector at every port in Canada where coal oil is imported ?
The inspection, I am informed is not a difficult matter. The officer has to weigh the oil, and an instrument is supplied for making the Hash test
That is the case in every port of entry where oil comes into Canada now ?
So the officer of the department informs me.
I am informed that Wallace-burg is a port of entry and that it receives oil, yet there is no one but the customshouse officer there, and there is no inspection.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) is wrong. That is not a customs port.
I understand that oil is received there constantly.
Not direct.
As I understand the Minister of Finance, oil is admitted at every port where there is a warehouse.
At every port which is known in the department as a warehousing port.
Is Brampton, Ontario, a warehousing port ?
I could not say. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) himself is probably aware.
I did not ask the question of the Minister of Finance.
I be" your pardon.

I asked it of the minister of the department.
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE I cannot answer the hon. gentleman's question. I have stated more than once that the customs officer has charge of the inspection of imported oil; my department has nothing to do with it .
Will the minister give the House a list of the warehousing ports in Ontario where oil is received by tank ?
I will ask the Minister of Customs to subtly that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: There is a dispute among some of the members with respect to this matter. I understand that Port Perry and Clinton, which were mentioned by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) are not included among these ports. I think I am correct in that. Brampton, I understand, is not in this list of warehousing ports, and oil comes to that place in barrels, as under the old Act. But I think it is only fair to the committee that we should be supplied with a list of the ports for Ontario or for the Dominion.
That will be brought down.
I suppose the hon. member (Mr. Blain) will take my word for it that tank wagons visit Port Perry ?
Yes.

As I understand, we have been talking about oil imported from the United States. It is not against the law to bring oil from the United States in barrels, and it is still brought in that way, as well as in tanks. Dealers bring it in tanks to avoid the cost of transportation and leakage. Oil in tanks would bo inspected to see that it is all right The dealer would be responsible if it were reduced by adulteration. On the other hand, if an importer brought oil in ban-els, it would be the duty of the inspector to stamp the barrel. But it would be impossible to put a stamp on every gallon In a tank car. The tank car comes to a place where they have a large receiving tank, and, from this it is taken into the tank wagons and distributed throughout the country.
Is Port Perry a port of entry ?
No, Whitby is our port.
Would the hon. gentleman state where this wagon gets its supply to take to Port Perry ?
I think it comes from Toronto or from Whitby.

If the special test ordered by the minister of the oil from the Northwest does not disclose the fact that the oil submitted to the test is faulty, then there will be no legislation, I suppose ?
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE I did not say that. We will deal with the matter when the report comes in.

The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) struck the nail upon the head. It is clear that a large quantity of petroleum was imported into the Northwest which was not an illuminating oil.
It is clear that that oil should not have entered this country for the purpose for which it was imported unless it could stand a certain test. It must be equally clear that the department passed that oil.
Not at -all.

This is not a solitary case. This oil that would neither burn nor give light, was distributed over a large territory. There is a clause in the old Act, and, I presume, of the new, that the oil shall be inspected when it enters the country. This oil was undoubtedly inspected by the officer of the department, yet, it is clear that it could not stand the test required of an illuminating oil. What does he do ? He puts on the package certain figures, a certain flash test, a specific gravity ; and he knows whether the figures show that it is good illuminating oil. But the public do not know, they only see certain figures there. The inspector may send forward to the public oil that, on the face of it, is bad, and yet the public, unless they could get the hon. member for West York to travel around with his little paper and define to them whether the figures show good oil or not, are in perfect ignorance. If that is the effect of the statute, it ought to be altered, so that an inspector shall not pass any oil that does not stand the test for a good illuminating oil.

Regarding the statement I made just now, I am correct. Oil is brought into Wallaceburg in barrels and landed on the wharf without inspection. It pays customs duty, and is then free to be sent all over this country, no matter what the character of the oil may be. There is no inspection, there is no means of inspection. I understand the oil that is used in the Northwest is almost entirely supplied in barrels and not in tanks. Now it is quite possible there may be many ports like Wallaceburg where oil is delivered by boat, not tank oil but barrel oil, brought into this country and simply dumped on the wharf, where it pays duty, and is passed. It is passed now without any brand on the barrel. I understand in this way it is quite possible that large quantities of very inferior oil may be delivered in Canada and find its way to the North-west. I do not know that that is the case, but it is quite possible, and exceedingly probable; I think I am quite safe in saying that as regards this one port there is no inspection of oil delivered there in barrels.

If the hon. gentleman's statement is correct it needs investigation, and I shall call the attention of the Minister of Customs to it. It is not the intention of the law, and it should not happen. Since the hon. gentleman makes the statement as a matter coming within his knowledge, the Minister of Customs will be bound to look into it and see what is the answer, if there be one.

The hon. member for Bothwell knows that Wallaceburg is not a port of entry, and that the oil supplied at
Wallaceburg is either entered at some other port probably Chatham, or is smuggled in. If entered at any other port it is inspected the same as it would be if it were in tanks.

I am surprised that the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) does not know that Wallaceburg is a port of entry. It is an astounding revelation to me. Wallaceburg has been a port of entry for more than 30 years, I venture to say for 40 years. There are several outports at Wallaceburg. The village of Sombra and the village of Tort Lambton are outports, and AVallaceburg is just as much a port of entry as the city of Chatham. If it is anything to boast of, it is quite as great as Chatham. What has been stated by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) is perfectly true. I am not prepared to say whether instructions have been given the collector of customs there to make an inspection. But I have personal knowledge that oil is brought in from the United States, from Detroit and from little towns on the border, is entered with the collector of customs, and duty paid, and no attempt made at inspection. I am not now making a charge against the collector there, I do not know whether he had such instructions, but that has been the experience at that port, no doubt about it.
What I meant to say was that Wallaceburg was not a warehousing port. As the inspection of oil comes under the Customs Department, it could not be inspected at Wallaceburg.
I would like to ask the minister if that regulation regarding stamps to go on the end of the barrel, has been abolished ?
Yes.
Then will the hon. gentleman state, when coal oil comes from the United States in small barrels, if it is tested, and by whom ?
When it is imported in tanks, either in bar-rals or otherwise-I have already read the law-it must be inspected by the customs officer.

In order to relieve a part of the strain that appears to exist in regard to the regulations as to the inspection of oil from the United States, I beg to say that according to my best information the principal part of the oil of which complaint was made in the North-west, was Canadian oil ; it was brought in tank vessels to Port William, was placed in large tanks and barrelled there for distribution throughout Manitoba and the North-west.

Has the hon. gentleman knowledge of that ? The hon. gentleman

has made a very serious charge against the refiners of oil in Canada. I may tell him that they would have to send it in by tank cars, probably to the town of Sarnia in the first place, for shipment, and then they would have to re-ship it in tank vessels. Unless the hon. gentleman has personal knowledge of the accuracy of that statement, it is unfair to the oil producers in Canada.
I have no hesitation in taking the responsibility of stating that a large part of the oil complained of in the Northwest during the past five months was sold as Canadian oil.
That is another thing.

I did not follow the oil from the well to the lamp. But I can assure the hon. member that it was Canadian oil, and for the information of other hon. members I may say that Canadian oil holds a very bad pre-eminence in reputation in the Northwest. It is not considered to be as good as American oil. As a matter of fact, however, the oil brought to Fort William was there placed in large tanks and there barrelled for distribution throughout the North-west. That is the history of the greater part of the oil trade of the west.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that his information is entirely wrong. There is not a tank vessel owned by a single individual in Canada. When the hon. gentleman states that it has a bad reputation, I am afraid that it is owing entirely to his conduct in the past. He and his party decried Canadian oil for the purpose of making capital out of it as against American oil. The hon. gentleman, I am afraid, has given it a bad reputation and circulated the reputation throughont the country. I want to say to him that it is utterly unfair for the hon. gentleman to make the statement in this House that Canadian oil is sent in tank vessels to the upper lakes and then reshipped to the North-west. I think the hon. gentleman is utterly without a tittle of foundation for his statement, and I hope that he will soon acquire the necessary information and make the correction.

I will take the responsibility of stating here in this House, and now, that from Lake Superior to the Pacific Ocean, now and heretofore, the reputation of Canadian oil is absolutely inferior to that of American oil.

In regard to the matter that has been referred to by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), I have this to say, that Mr. Sharpe, the present manager of the Standard Oil Company, certainly stated in his interview in the paper, as may be seen in the ' Telegram ' of about the 20th of November, and I heard his son on a public platform assert, that it was American oil. Now, Mr. Chairman, it is rather amusing to

listen to the flippant remarks of some hon. members from Ontario referring to us as being in the dark. We certainly were in the dark in 1896, and previously, regarding the party and the government that have had charge of the coal oil legislation for the past few years. I would like that my hon. friend had been with the premier when he traversed that country from the Red River to the Rocky Mountains, as no doubt the member for Alberta was, and had seen the placards on every wall where he spoke, and where he bewailed the position of the people of that country with regard to the coal oil tax, that he promised to wipe out immediately, and which he has so enormously reduced by one cent a gallon. Then certain arrangements were made whereby the Standard Oil Company was permitted to come into this country and get control of the market, as has been shown by members from both sides of the House, and that, Mr. Chairman, after the government was warned from this side of the House, warned, if I mistake not, by the late member for West York (Mr. Wallace), that what has happened would happen.
To provide for extra duty pay at large distilleries and other factories, $6,000.
This vote is the same as last year, and for three or four years preceding.
How much of that vote of last year was spent ?

Last year, out of that vote of 86,000, we expended 85,701.02.
Salaries of officers, inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures, $55,100.

I think it is time now that we should have some explanation from the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue as to the conduct of his officers, because I fear, from the results we have had, that they have disobeyed the orders sent out by the department. Either the inspectors have been remiss in their duty or the hon. gentleman has modified the instructions that I am informed were sent to the inspectors throughout the country in regard to the use of what is known as the grain tester. I understand that a deputation waited on the hon. gentleman from the grain section of the board of trade of the city of Toronto and remonstrated against what they called a departmental regulation, but which, of course, was a statute instead of a departmental regulation. The hon. gentleman has not, apparently, taken great trouble to see that his officers have discharged their duty. I would like some declaration on the hon. gentleman's part making it perfectly plain, either that he is, as minister, utterly helpless to enforce the law by reason of the inspectors being remiss in their duty, or that the hon. gentleman is disposed to give a willing ear

118&
to those who are contending against the operation of such a law. I shall await the hon. gentleman's explanation of what is to me and to the whole country a very extraordinary state of affairs, namely, that there has been a law on the statute-book for something over five years, that the inspector who was instructed to enforce that law has not done so, and that so far as the inspection is concerned, it is absolutely and utterly a dead letter. 1 never knew a case where the law has been so completely ignored and I am sure the committee and the country will be delighted to know what are the underlying reasons for such an extraordinary state of affairs.

I think I had better, in order that the committee may be in a position to discuss the matter more fully and with perfect knowledge, give a short history in regard to the question referred to by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). Grain testers were admitted to verification by .Order in Council of August 20th, 1881. See circular No. 238. The Department of Justice decided in 1889 that grain testers were liable to inspection under the Weights and Measures Act. See circular G, 300, and copy of opinion of Department of Justice attached. In the spring of 1890, the department decided owing to the pressure from all points, to ask l'or the repeal of the Order in Council, permitting their verification. The farmers, on the one hand, urged that verification be not permitted, while boards of trade desired them to be admitted to inspection. By an Order in Council of June 7th, 1890, the previous order admitting grain testers to verification was repealed. See circular G 324. By 01 Vic., chap. 30, section 6, subsection 2, it was provided that ' no weighing machine used for weighing or determining the weights of any of the articles mentioned in section 10 of the Weights and Measures Act shall be of less certified capacity than one bushel.' See circular G 588, calling attention to the above quoted amendment and directing inspectors to acquaint persons who are using those measures, of the penalties attached for not complying with the law.
A circular was again issued by the department in September, 1901, calling attention, a further time, to the provisions of the Act 01 Vic., chap. 30. See circular G 023. The grain tester is used only to determine tlie weight of grain per bushel, not the actual weight of a given quantity offered for sale. It is, in fact, a test of quality, not of quantity, the grain so tested as to quality having subsequently to be weighed on verified scales when bought and sold. Until the amendment of 1898, the department took the stand that, as the grain, in respect of which the quality is determined by the tester, is sold by actual weight on legalized scales it had no right to interfere with the use of the tester, ns the seller can decline to accept the tester as an arbiter. It thus being an 38
unrecognized weighing machine no contract could be determined by it, but that nothing could prevent millers and others using it for their own information.

Does the hon. gentleman state that the law does not interfere with any persons attempting to make a test in any vessels of less than one bushel certified capacity ? The reading of the statute is just what the hon. gentleman said, but the hon. gentleman has expressed some view outside of the statute that I am not quite clear about.

Until the amendment of 1898, the department took the stand that as the grain in respect of which the quality is determined by the tester is sold by actual weight on legalized scales it had no right to interfere with the use of the tester as the seller can decline to accept the tester as an arbiter.
Do I understand that to be a departmental regulation ?
No.

How does the hon. gentleman arrive at the conclusion that since the grain is sold subject to being weighed on legalized scales the department could not prevent the use of the tester under such circumstances, because the seller might decline to have it tested. I want to say that there is no complaint against the test. The complaint is against the use of a tester of less certified capacity than one bushel. I do not understand that there has been any amendment of the Act of 1898 affecting that part of it :
No weighing machine used for weighing or determining the weights of any of the articles mentioned in section 16 of the Weights and Measures Act shall be of less certified capacity than one bushel.
The test is made so as to see that the wheat is standard, and if the wheat is below standard there is a scale fixed by which an arbitrary reduction is made on the price of each bushel. Whether grain is bought or sold, the person has absolutely no right to make a test with any tester of less certified capacity than one bushel. Judging by the remarks of the minister, I can well understand why the law has been absolutely ignored.
Grain testers are used by the buyers to test the quality, and the seller is not bound to accept the decision of the buyer even after that test.
Yes, he is. At every mill door and warehouse door he had to accept it or turn his team back and take it home. In theory the minister is right, but as a matter of practice he is wrong.
I was always of the opinion, and I still hold the same opinion, that the least we intervene in private business the better.
speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVEN HE.

speechtext: Now, the country will understand for the first time the position of the minister.

These tests were not the exact measure by which the quality or quantity was to be returned. I cannot understand why the seller would be bound to accept the terms of the buyer even if he had to take his grain home.
Quite so; no hardship in that.

I do not understand how trade is conducted in the province of Ontario, but I know something of that matter in the province of Quebec. We use what we call a half bushel. If a farmer has 500 or 600 bushels of oats or peas for sale, he goes to the buyer and he says to him : I am ready to sell you 500 bushels of oats to be delivered within a month or two. When he has delivered the oats or peas the value is determined, not by the bushel, but by the weight according to law. That is the rule In the province of Quebec, and it is not to niy knowledge that any lawsuit was ever instituted because there was a misunderstanding between the parties. If the facts are as represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) I suppose it remains that we should change the law.
No. Enforce it.
Perhaps it would be in order that a Bill should be introduced so that we may test the sentiment of the House and of the country.

The people who complain do not ask that the law should be altered, but they ask that it should be enforced. The minister proposes now to submit a Bill to the House to test public opinion on the question as to whether the present law should be enforced or not I cannot understand what the hon. gentleman means. I tell the minister that there is absolutely no complaint against the law, which is efficient; but there is a complaint that the law is not enforced. The minister says that he does not care to interfere with private transactions, but I tell him that this is a public transaction. So far as my knowledge goes, there is no such a thing as grain tests in the United States or in any other province of the Dominion except Ontario. I am not opposed to the test. If I were engaged in the grain business I think I should want to determine the value of grain by a tester. Whait I am asking is that if a grain tester is to be used at all, Mr. CLANCY.
and I do not say it should not, that grain tester shall not be of a less capacity than one certified bushel. We simply ask the minister to have backbone enough to enforce the law. When he suggests a change in the law I am afraid that he is giving a willing ear to the deputation that thundered at the door of his office recently asking that the law should be repealed. If the minister wants to tinker with the law now, it is only for the purpose of crippling it so that it may be of no use to the farmer. I hope that I have made myself clear as to the views of the farmers of Ontario generally on this question.
In the town I come from, most of the grain buyers if not all of them, are using bushel measures to test the grain.
When did the hon. gentleman get that information ?
My firm has made a good many good dozens of these measures for the grain buyers, lor at least the last year.
If the hon. gentleman will wire to the principal buyers in this town I venture to say he will find that is not the case. I have it from the farmers themselves.

Well, whether the hon. member (Mr. Clancy) says it is the case or not, that will not alter the fact. I say that when the farmer sells his grain he brings it to the buyer, and the buyer tests with the bushel measure as I have seen myself, and our firm have made that measure, and we have been selling it for the last year. The farmer can make his bargain in selling his grain just as he does in selling his cattle. He can say to the buyer :	I
will sell you a thousand bushels of wheat, but you are to take this wheat at its actual weight; you are to use no tester. If the man says he wants it tested the farmer can say that he will not have it, and so the farmer can make a bargain when selling his grain the same as he can when selling his stock or any product of the farm.

I hear some hon. gentlemen cheering, and they seem to make it their business behind there to chatter out ' Hear, Hear,' on every occasion. I do not wish to be offensive to these gentlemen, but I wish to say to the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Stephens) that notwithstanding he makes his measures, and sells them, the fact remains that gentlemen of quite as reputable character as his-and his character is a good one-have stated to me within the last two months that the tester was being used as formerly. If the hon. gentleman denies that, he casts a reflection on the statement made to me by most reputable farmers. I am sure that if the farmers in his constituency read his state-

ment in the press to-morrow that for the last year nothing but the bushel test has been used, it will be a great surprise to them. 1 have not seen the small tester used, but I have scarcely been a day in the city of Chatham, that farmers of reputation and truth and respectability have not told me within the last two or three months, that the old tester of one-sixteenth of a bushel is being used. I have no hesitation in accepting the statement of gentlemen who are just as respectable and just as truthful as any member in this House.
I have sold grain myself during the last year, and it was not tested.
That might be.

There was no bargain as to test when I sold the grain. They weighed it in and gave me so much per bushel on that weight. I have been among the farmers probably as much as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has been, and I have yet to hear one recent complaint tnat the small tester is being used in the city of Chatham.

I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman say that, and I hope it will appear in the newspapers to-morrow.
Mr. McEWEN; I happen to be a grain merchant, and I know that in our locality the inspector sent a circular to the grain men and also to the millers forbidding them to use the tester, and since then I have put away mine. I do not know how many others have done the same thing. The grain inspector also said, that if he came around and found any in use he would confiscate them. I believe they are done away with in our section. At all events they are forbidden and liable to be confiscated.

I am very glad to hear that statement, and I hope it will apply generally, but my information is that it does not. I am aware that the minister has sent out a circular, but the annoying part of it is that in some localities at least there has been no attention paid to it. I am told that in my own town the small tester is in use still.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Kent what material is used in the manufacture of those bushel measures ?
Light steel.
Are they stamped ?
Yes, by the government inspector.
What kind of a bottom ?
Wood or iron, or any other material, so long as it is of the right size.

I consider this bushel measure a great mistake. On a cold winter 3Si
day, when half a dozen or more teams are waiting to be unloaded, you have to take a bushel and fill it out of every man's sleigh, and weigh it. I can assure you it is a very great hardship. The majority of grain men would rather trust their eyes than go to that trouble. The men who find * the most fault with these small grain testers are those with light grain ; these are the men who make the loudest noise. The grain tester is a good thing for both the grain men and the grain merchant, and I think that is the proper thing to use.
As a grain producer and seller, I can say that it is the small measure which was used in Cardwell, Charleston, Caledon East, Mono Road and Bolton last fall.

Before we vote the salaries for these inspectors, I think we might now ask for some declaration on the part of the minister as to whether he still adheres to the statement he made a moment ago that he did not care to interfere, as he thought it would be an interference with trade. We might reasonably expect a statement from the hon. gentleman that he will see that the Act is enforced rather than propose any amendments to it.

I may say to my hon. friend that in order to have the law carried out, and perhaps at his own instance, we issued on the 10th of September, 1901, the following circular : Department of Inland Revenue.
Sir,-Complaint has been made to the department that notwithstanding the provision of subsection 2 of section 6 of 61 Victoria, chapter 30, the law is being contravened (already brought to your notice by circular sheet 588 of March 9, 1900.) This section reads as follows :
'No weighing machine used for weighing or determining the weights of any of the articles mentioned in section 16 of the Weights and Measures Act shall be of less capacity than one bushel.'
Therefore, any use made of any weighing machine (having a less capacity than one bushel) for the purpose of charging for or ascertaining the amount or price to be paid for any of the articles referred to in section 16, is illegal. It Is the duty of all Inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures to so advise all persons offending, and to notify them that the further illegal use of such weighing machines shall lead to their confiscation and to the institution of proceedings for the collection of the penalties fixed by section 29 of said Act.
This Is the circular that was issued last year. I may add that I was not in a position to judge of the merits or demerits of that grain tester. Some of the dealers are in favour of using it, and I cannot perceive now why, in face of the law and our circular, a farmer should be bound to sell his grain to a man who uses a grain tester. On the one hand, we have the representation of the hon. member for Bothwell, who may be sustained by the opinion of some other gentlemen ; but, on the other hand,

we have the boards of trade, representing the buyers and shippers, who want us to maintain the use of the grain tester.
The small one ?

Yes. I may say to my hon. friend, en passant, that I was never approached by any deputation. We have received resolutions passed by the boards of trade in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and perhaps some other places ; but, without entering into the merits of the use of the grain tester, would my hon. friend say that it would be in the interest of the farmers of Manitoba ?

They are not interfered with at all, because it is not used there. They have their grain standards, which are fixed by persons whose business it is to establish the qualities of the grain. There is no such thing as this small grain tester used anywhere in Canada outside of the province of Ontario.

What is the hon. gentleman asking us to do ? We have issued a circular according to the law as amended in 1901. and we have told our officers that they should inform people using those testers that if they continue doing so the penalties enacted by the law will he imposed. The hon. gentleman now wants us to take legal proceedings ; but if that grain tester is not illegal, how can we succeed ?
Has any one contended that it is a legal measure ?

It cannot be legal, because the clause of the Act which I have already read says that no measure less than a bushel shall be used. Suppose we were to take an action, what would be the result of it ? The man would say. ' I may use a grain tester or any other kind of measure/ It is not the fact that the little instrument bears the name of grain tester that makes it legal. You can use any other vessel.
That law declares that any other cannot be used.
Yes, but that it is a matter of private bargain between the buyer and seller.
No.
Yes, because they agree upon a certain measure not to determine the weight or the quality, but to form a basis for arranging the price. That is a matter of private bargain.

It is not often that we find a minister of the Crown declaring his utter helplessness to enforce the law. Any tester less than a bushel is false weight or measure-it is a false instrument for the purpose under the law, and it is the duty of

the hon. minister, at any cost, to see that the law is enforced in this case as in any other. The hon. gentleman need not enter into any question of testing it in the courts. He has only to say to his officers to see to it that there are none of these instruments in use, and that any that are found in use shall be confiscated and any who use them fined. Would the hon. gentleman have the farmer bring before the courts a man whom he found using one of these instruments, entering upon a lawsuit that would probably cost him his farm in fighting a great corporation like the Millers' Association ? Or is he prepared to take the course, the only course that is open to a minister, particularly when he has asked the House to vote money to pay the officers to enforce the law, and that is to enforce that law fairly. There is no need to bandy words about it. It is as plain as anything could be made that there is a law in the statute-book which forbids the use of such an instrument. I will do the hon. minister the credit of saying that he is making laudable efforts to carry out the law. But he tells us that they are fruitless, and that seems to end his inclination to carry out the law. It is not a matter of private bargain, because there is no bargain made. Suppose that the hon. minister is a grain buyer. I go to his warehouse with a load of grain. I make no bargain, except to sell for 75 cents a bushel, subject to a test which may either increase or lower the price. This is not a matter of private bargain, but an appeal to the law where there is no bargain, and where no bargain need to be made. If I said I would sell my grain at 75 cents per bushel, regardless of what tlie tester might make it, whether above or below the standard, that might fairly be called a matter of bargain. But where tin; price may be varied according to the results shown by the tester under the rules of the Millers' Association, that is a different matter. I repeat what I have often said, that I do not object to the grain-buyer having a means of testing the grain he is buying from the farmer. But I venture to repeat that it is clear that it is not for the minister to inquire whether the farmer has made a bargain or not where this tester has been used. The fact is a false weight or measure prohibited by the law has been used, and it is the duty of the officers to take cognizance of that fact. I would ask the hon. minister if he is preparing to follow up the pfforts he has made for the enforcement of the present law ? I had some information that the inspectors are not sent out especially for this business as a rule. I do not know whether they are sent out specially in any case or not, but, no doubt the minister will be able to inform us. I understand that the inspection is not made oftener than once a year. If no inspector is sent out, I can understand that the law will be ignored, because this matter will never come under the notice of the in spec-

tors whose special duty it is to inspect weights and measures, but whose additional duty it is to look after this tester. I think the hon. minister has made a laudable effort.
I think he took the only step that could be taken by a minister-he tried to enforce the law. I think I ought to have some declaration from him whether he will, if necessary, send out inspectors especially to see to this matter and enforce the law. Anything short of that means that the law will not be enforced.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before the minister answers my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) I would like to ask both the minister and my hon. friend how the law would be enforced in such a case ? I have been in the grain business for thirty years. This tester, as my hon. friend calls it, was purchased by the grain-buyers some years ago, when we dealt largely in barley to export to the United - States. If, according to the tester, that barley weighed forty-six pounds a bushel, it was worth so much; if it weighed forty-eight or 50 pounds, it would be worth so much more. In order to be able to get our barley graded we invested in these American weighing machines.
They are not American.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I bought mine in the United States. The instrument consisted of a funnel, and the grain filtered down into a two-quart measure that hung on a scale. When it was filled through the funnel, you struck it off level with a ruler, and you were then able to see what the barley weighed per bushel. The farmers, of course, objected, that if they filled the bushel measure and then struck the side of the measure, it would contain more and show a greater weight per bushel. This raised a cry against these machines, and this regulation was adopted. I have one of those machines in my warehouse. A man comes to me with a load of grain, and we bargain as to the price. What is to prevent me taking a sample of that grain into my office to examine it and ascertain its value. I fill my two-quart measure and come to the conclusion that the grain is worth 70 cents per bushel. I offer that price to the farmer, and he is free to take it or not, as he pleases. I deny the right of the government or anybody else to take that instrument, which is my property, out of my warehouse and smash it. I am not buying or selling by it. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, the grain is bought on an examination of a sample held in the hand. But, sometimes a case arises when we want to know the weight per bushel, and that is what the tester is used for. It is not used as a test between buyer and seller, but it is used by the buyer as a means of ascertaining what the grain is worth.
Then, why does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) object to this ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is my property, and I am not using it in any illegal way. Therefore, I deny the right of this government or anybody else to take it from me.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has convicted himself. He says he does not buy or sell by this instrument. Yet he says also that he uses this test before he tells the farmers what he will give them for the grain. Now, there is no gentleman would dare to assume the responsibility of defending a measure that is found to be false. I am not accusing the grain men of endeavouring to cheat. But if the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to go to the Department of Inland Revenue when the test was made by the minister and deputy minister with wheat weighing 62| pounds per bushel, he would have seen that after the test had been made of a bushel by the small tester, that there was still ten and one-half ounces left. Why? Because it was dribbled through that little funnel, the air was allowed to get in, and the vessel was too small, and it turned out to be a false test. What was that test, as it would have operated on the farmer ? There were only five out of sixteen tests that went to 62 pounds, although it was 62} pounds by actual weight in a bushel tester, and in a bushel measure. Now, eleven of those farmers would have to take 61 pounds out of the sixteen tests. I think that my hon. friend, although a very just man, has been on one side of the question all his life. He had better read again what the law declares. The section reads : No weighing machine used tor weighing or determining the weight of any articles mentioned in section 16 of the Weights and Measures Act, shall be of less certified capacity than one bushel.
The hon. gentleman uses one-sixteentli of a bushel. Now it has been found by actual experience-and I make no charge against those who use it-that it is so small that it is not a fair tester. The farmers do not ask that the men who purchase their grain should be deprived of the means of ascertaining the value of that grain by putting it into the test of a bushel. We all concede that it is not so convenient ; but it cannot be urged that on the ground of convenience a measure should be used that is not fair to the farmer.
Do I understand that the only measure that can be used in the province of Ontario between the buyer and seller of grain is a one-bushel measure ?
The legal measure, the law says so.
And only a bushel measure?
Yes.

Suppose a farmer went into his neighbour's granary and purchased 30 bushels of wheat, would he he compelled to

use a one-bushel measure to measure that wheat ?

They are bound to use It. They have always to go to the legal weight. I mentioned the practice in Quebec. There we use the term bushel in speaking of 400 bushels, 500 bushels, 600 bushels or any other quantity. But when we come to deliver the grain it is always by weight according to the agreement between seller and buyer. The buyer will say, I will give you 25 cents, or 30 cents, for 32, 34 or 36 pounds of oats. That is the condition of sale, always understood.
Not always in Montreal, for weight.

They may change it in Montreal. Sometimes they say 40 pounds or 42 pounds. It depends on the weight of the oats, which is not always the same. In some years the oats are heavier than in other years. But I cannot understand, in face of the law as it is to-day, how far we can go, and I call the attention of the legal profession here to that point.	*
Cannot the hon. gentleman see that the instructions are carried out ?

Yes, but then we will be face to face with the argument used by the hon member ior Leeds (Mr. Taylor) :	Can you deprive me
of my measure ? The government has no business to interfere.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not use this tester in buying grain by any means. I have a two-quart measure, I fill that two-quart measure, and I set it on the scales to see how much it will weigh. That is what a grain man does. One load of oats may weigh 40 pounds to the bushel, another load 32 pounds ; that which weighs 40 pounds is worth more than that which weighs but 32 pounds, and this instrument will indicate it to me.
Why not use a bushel ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because it is not so convenient. Ninety-nine loads out of 100 are bought by the purchaser merely looking at the grain in his hand. There is not a grain man in Ontario but has one of these instruments in his warehouse.

The hon. gentleman says he does not set the law at defiance. the hon. member for Leeds says he just uses it when he likes. If he uses it at all the law declares it shall be a bushel. He is not obliged to use it, but the farmer ought to be protected when he does use it, and know that it has a certified capacity of one bushel. Yet the hon. gentleman declares that he cannot be prevented from using a tester. Unless the tester is of the certified capacity of one bushel he is using it illegally, because Mr. BLAIN.
the measure is his own it gives him no right to use it. The hon. gentleman is not obliged to use a tester, but if he does use one, the law steps in and says, for the protection of the farmer, that it must be one bushel.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And that is all right. My hon. friend comes to me and says, I want to sell you 500 bushels of pease, or wheat, and if your wheat weighs 60 pounds a bushel I will give you 80 cents a bushel. He comes in with his wheat and I must then take a bushel measure and put it on the scales and test it. But if he comes in with his load of grain and says : How much will you give me for that load of grain, without saying anything about the weight, I look at it, and if I am not satisfied as to what it will weigh, I take two quarts of it and weigh it and make the calculation to see how much a bushel will weigh, and I pay for it accordingly. But if I buy from a man and he guarantees me that his oats will weigh 34 pounds a bushel, I must, by the law, use a one-bushel measure.
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I say yes. You come to me to sell me 500 bushels of oats, and I say I will give you 30 cents a bushel if they weigh 34 pounds to the bushel. Then I must weigh a bushel. But if I am buying these from you and nothing said about the quantity, or the quality, I look at the oats, and I may be deceived, I may think these oats will not weigh over 30 pounds.
I will take two quarts and test them for my satisfaction, and the result will tell me whether they will weigh 30 or 32 or 34 pounds to the bushel. That is all we use it for. But if I buy oats at a price of so much per bushel provided they weigh 34 pounds, I must weigh one bushel to see how much they will weigh. But in the case of every load of grain that comes in after we make the bargain, it is put on the platform scales and the quantity is thus determined.

The hon, gentleman need not try to confuse the question. A man brings in a load of grain. The hon. gentleman wants to be sure that it is up to a certain standard, and he takes his two quart measure and by that he makes the test. The complaint of the farmer is not that he takes grain without a test, because he will be glad to sell it and to take so much for his grain to be weighed on the scale and no test. But the buyer insists upon the test, he asks that it shall be made in a vessel, namely, a bushel measure, and it has been demonstrated time and again that nothing else than that is fair. Now, I want to ask the hon. minister to declare to the House whether he intends to continue in his efforts to enforce the Act as it now stands.
Yes.

It seems to me this question resolves Itself Into ascertaining whether the minister has power or not to take these vessels away from the grain buyers. I myself have made some inquiry, and I believe he has not that power, and that the grain buyer can use this tester to satisfy himself the same as he can use his eyes to satisfy himself. He does not use it for the purpose of buying grain from the * farmer, but to satisfy himself as to its value. I believe that a tester is a good thing, but it should be a bushel measure.
I think if the minister has the power he should do away with the smaller measure altogether, but I do not believe that he has power to do that. I believe that the buyer can use the tester the same as he can use his eyes.
As I understand the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) he proposes that the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue should destroy all the testing machines of less than one bushel capacity.
No.

I thought the hon. gentleman said that. If the minister were to do that it would inflict a very great hardship on a great many people. I buy a carload of flax seed, for instance, and I test it with a machine very much smaller than one bushel capacity. We have to ascertain how much dirt there is in that flax, and it is understood in the trade that it'shall be sold subject to that test. It would be a very great hardship to adopt a bushel measure for this purpose. I hope the hon. member will not destroy all of these machines that are of a less capacity than one bushel.

My hon. friend (Mr. McGowan) misunderstands me. I can assure him that I am not so belligerent as he suspects. All I ask the hon. gentleman to do is to put that machine aside and buy a new one of a bushel capacity.
Well, I will not do that.
I did not hear what the hon. member said in response to my question a moment ago.
I said that I would endeavour to have the law carried out.
Has the hon. gentleman any special inspection for this purpose ?
No, except that the officers will have to comply with the circular that I have already read.

I had a promise from the hon. gentleman's department that inspectors at least within a limited area would go out for this purpose, I want to ask the hon. gentleman if this promise has been carried out.	.
That was done.

The grievance that the farmer feels against the use of a smaller measure than one bushel is tliis :	You go in with your load of grain
and the merchant tells you he will give you so much if it comes up to such a test and he shows you a sample of grain which is sent to him as a standard to go by. The farmer thinks that the grain should be tested in a larger vessel than is used so that the balance would have to be counted upon when weighing because it always takes something to balance the beam in weighing a quantity short of a bushel. I think it would be fairer that there should be one bushel weighed because the merchant has an advantage in weighing a little at a time instead of a whole bushel. We all know very well that it takes something to balance the beam always and whilst you weigh oftener it will count that when you come up to the amount of a bushel. I do not know whether the department will be able to confiscate these small machines or not. I believe there is no use in attempting it unless it can compel each buyer to test the grain in a bushel measure.

Mr. Chairman, there is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Inland Revenue with the object of getting his views upon it. It is the matter of the weighing of grain coming through threshing machines. I do not know whether this question has reached the attention of the hon. minister or not, but it is a matter of a great deal of importance to the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. According to the way in which the Weights and Measures Act has been interpreted I understand that the owners of grain have to pay for their threshing by the bushel measure. Most of the threshing machines in Manitoba and the North-west Territories have bushellers that put the grain into a bag and. the bags are counted, or they have automatic weighers that weigh the grain as it is threshed, and passed up through an elevator. I am told by men engaged in the business that they have a great deal of trouble with some dishonest people in collecting the amount of their threshing bills, because, after threshing has been done, iii some cases, they have refused to pay for it, claiming that, according to the regulation of the Department of Inland Revenue, they are not called upon to pay for any grain which is not measured through a bushel measure. If that is the correct interpretation of the Act, I think it is decidedly a great hardship to the men engaged in the threshing business. I understand there have been some cases before the courts in the province of Manitoba and that decisions such as I have referred to against the grain threshers have been given in the manner which I have mentioned. I would

like to have the opinion of the hon. minister in regard to it.

We hare already had a reference of the matter to the department. There were complaints that a dispute had arisen between the proprietors of these threshing machines and some farmers, but this is one of those cases with which we cannot interfere. Our answer was that we were not prepared, to devise a machine by which an apparatus might be provided to be attached to a threshing machine for the purpose of weighing grain. Let the farmers and the men who manage these machines agree upon some kind of a measure or weighing machine which we can inspect. All we can do is to inspect that measure or weighing machine. The manufacturer of these machines cannot expect the department to devise a means by which an apparatus can be attached to a machine such as a weighing machine or some kind of a measure. That is not our business. I cannot understand why the owners of threshing machines and the farmers cannot agree as to that. We have, in the province of Quebec, threshing machines, perhaps not so powerful as these, and I never heard that there was any dispute in regard to the payment to the owners of those machines. This is a question that they must settle for themselves. We cannot 'inspect unless we are called upon to inspect a measure.

The hon. minister states that he does not see any reason why the threshers and the farmers cannot have some measure that they can mutually agree upon. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) has referred to the fact that by some decisions of the courts they cannot do this. I am in receipt of some communications from threshers, amongst them is one from the secretary of the Threshers Protective Association ' in which they state they are not permitted to do that.
I will read one letter I have received :
I beg leave to call your attention to the bearing the Weights and Measures Act has on thresbermen. According to a late decision a thresherman cannot collect unless he uses1 a standard measure which must be stricken, a thing it is almost impossible to do. As a thresher does not buy grain but only bestows a certain amount of labour upon it in preparing it for market he should be allowed to contract by bag or any way that will be mutally agreeable the same as any other labourers who take part in its production. Mr. Si [ton was interviewed at Brandon, and promised to look into the matter and we would ask you to give your aid and assistance when it comes up.
The hon. gentleman will see that the secretary of the Threshers Protective Association is under the impression that they cannot enter into an agreement that will be mutually satisfactory on account of this decision.

Let these men agree among themselves on a measure and we are ready to inspect that measure. But, we cannot go further. They want us to devise some means by way of an apparatus attached to the threshing machine. We cannot do that. It is only our duty to inspect weights or measures under the law.
Do I understand the hon. [DOT] minister to say that they will not inspect this measure that is on the machine ?

No. We cannot inspect a measure attached to the threshing machine unless it comes under the terms of the law. If it does, then of course we are bound to inspect it. Any machine which falls under the terms of the law we are bound to inspect.
