I think that would be a contradiction of the judgment which has been given by the courts if I understand it aright. I want to point out the hardship that these men are labouring under. These machines thresh from 2,000 up to 2,700 bushels in a day. How is it possible for wheat in quantities like that to be handled in any other way than the way in which it is now handled, either through a bagger, or through an automatic weigher ? We think the government should test these automatic weighing machines, or that some means should be devised whereby these men would be able to collect their charges for threshing grain.

I have not heard any explanation from the hon. minister as to why this increase of 10 per cent over the vote for last year is asked for.
Is it caused by an increase In the number of officers or, have the salaries been increased ?

I will give the information to my hon. friend. There is an increase of $4,950, made up as follows : It is in the first place to provide for the inspection of weights and measures in the Yukon, where we have no inspection now, and there is pressure brought to bear that we should appoint an officer, which I think we should do.
Will he do his duty ?

I expect so. To appoint an inspector in St. Hyaclnthe, $800; to appoint Thomas Parker, assistant inspector, British Columbia mainland, $600; to provide an assistant inspector, Nova Scotia, $800; to appoint P. H. Prefon-taine, assistant inspector, Quebec, $500; to appoint .T. E. Bernier, assistant inspector, St. John, N.B., $600-I may say he is no relation of mine-increase to officers, $450; to transfer W. J. La belle from inside service to outside service, $1,100, making $6,350, less $1,400, leaving $4,950.
Metrical instruments, $500.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I had an application from the head master of the Gananoque High School a few days ago, for one of those metrical systems. I interviewed the minister in reference to the matter, and he told me that he had given a great many out to schools and that he had none on hand. The letter sent to me by the master of the Gananoque school says that this would be very useful to the pupils. In view of this, I believe that the minister should make provision in the supplementary estimates to secure a supply for the high schools of the Dominion. There are only one or two in each county. The government do very little for our schools, and I do not think they could spend money better than in furnishing all the high schools with these metrical charts.

As soon as the metric systems which have been ordered from France arrive here, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) will receive one for the academy for which he has applied. Since 1897-98 we have expended $1,750 for these metric systems. We have already given out 107 and we have application for . 43 more. Formerly we kept no record, but for two years we have a record giving the name of each institution to which they have been sent, and since 1 have been in the department they have been distributed to colleges, seminaries, convents, normal schools and high schools. It is the intention of the department to order some more to satisfy the demands.
Salaries of inspectors of gas ani electric light, $21,450.
Do these inspectors travel through country towns for the purpose of inspecting the electric light systems ?

The increase of $750 is for what may be called statutory increases, $400, and to appoint an inspector in Gharlottetown, $300. The inspection of electricity in done by the gas inspector in the town or locality when there is such an Officer, and when there is no such officer in the town the inspector of the next town makes the inspection.

Is it the duty of one of these inspectors to visit a country town where they have an electric light system at certain intervals during the year ?
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENuE. Whenever they are called for. The Act of last session provides that after the meters are fixed they remain untouched for five years except there is a disagreement between the user and the company. In that case the inspector is called in to examine the meter and he must do it in the presence of the owner or user. If there is no inspector in the locality, the parties interested or the company may call upon the officer in charge of the inspection in that district.
I refer more particularly to the towns in which there are no meters in use.
We inspect meters and not electric plant.
This item speaks of electric light inspectors.
That is the general term.
Do I understand that there is no electric light inspection in towns where no meters are used ?
They have to register in the department, and that is all.
This amount is considerable, and I do not want to refer to the discussion in respect to coal oil, which has occupied the greater part of the evening.
Hear, hear.

It seems to be the particular function of the hon. member for Bellecliasse to cry out ' hear, hear.' We are voting this evening over $600,000, a large part of which is for the inspection of gas and electric light. There is no doubt that a much larger proportion of the population use coal oil than use either of these illuminants. There have been complaints in the west and there have been great complaints around Montreal as to the quality of the coal oil sold. I believe the minister was right when he stated that as a matter of fact there is no inspection of coal oil, but I believe that he was wrong when he stated that the law does not authorize his department to inspect the illuminating xoower of coal oil. We have had a divergence of views on that. We have had the Minister of Finance say that the law did authorize the inspection, but I did not understand from the Minister of Justice that the law did authorize that inspection. My own idea, looking at the Act as I find it, is that your department has the power to make regulations which would enable you to inspect coal oil in the way we desire it should be inspected. Here is a company that has an immense sale of oil in Canada; it is a monopoly that carries out of the country over $2,000,000 a year in unfair profits, to my mind. It seems to me that we are entitled to know what the policy of the government is before we close this question. Is it the intention of the government to provide for such an inspection of coal oil as will ensure us a satisfactory quality ? If the government refuse to tell us what they are going to do in that respect, it is a proof that that gigantic company has even greater influence than we imagine it has.

I do not think so, and I do not think that my hon. friend is convinced of what he has said, that the company may have some power over the government or over myself.
I What I have said is that I will see how we

can remidy the evils complained of in Manitoba, the North-west or any other part of the Dominion ; and before proposing any change in the law, I will ascertain through the Department of Justice how far we can go under the law as it now stands. My hon. friend and myself might discuss the interpretation of the law, but that would have no practical result. What X have stated, and what I repeat, is that as soon as the report from Manitoba reaches us, which will be within two weeks, I shall have the whole question examined, to see what we can do to protect the public. I cannot say any more.
What was the result of the test of the first sample of coal oil brought from Manitoba ?
The result was that it was good oil.
Before this discussion is closed, I would like to say a few words. It seems to me that the mere presence of coal oil on the market is an indication that it has passed inspection by the government.
That is the assumption.

To thoroughly get over the difference it would be necessary to examine specimens of coal oil under the Adulteration of Food Act. There is no doubt whatever that it passes inspection in the first place, and if any manipulation takes place, it is while it is in transit to the retail dealer, or at all events before it reaches the consumer. As to Canadian oil being inferior to American oil, the suggestion is perfectly absurd. The best coal oil made on the continent to-day is Canadian oil. That is borne out by every possible test. Canadian water white oil is the best and most economical oil made. Its specific gravity is greater than that of American oil, it has less volatile matter, it burns as clearly, and lasts longer.
We certainly did not have that kind of oil in Manitoba last fall.
You said it was American oil.
If the hon. gentleman's statement be correct, it is very strange that the consumers in the province of Ontario will pay from two to five cents a gallon more for American oil than for Canadian oil.
It is beyond dispute that a great deal of Canadian water white oil is sold in Ontario as American oil.

If that is true, do you not think it requires some inspection ?
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, House adjourned at 12.05 a.m. Friday.
Friday, March 14, 1902.
